title: Javier Bardem & Penélope Cruz Talk Playing Fictitious Arguing Couple In ‘Bunker’:  “We Are Very Good At Creating Fiction & Reality” – Venice
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Renate Reinsve, Johnny Flynn & Vicky Krieps Set For Mia Hansen-Løve’s Mary Wollstonecraft Picture ‘If Love Should Die’ As Goodfellas Boards Sales – TIFF France & Korea Pledge $1.16B For Global Screen Industries At South Of France Cinema Summit Gaza Cinema Academy Launches At Venice Film Festival To Help Gazans Tell Their Own Stories View All September 8, 2026 6:25am Javier Bardem and Penélope Cruz attend Bunker Photocall at Venice Film Festival Kate Green/Getty Images A-list couple Penélope Cruz and Javier Bardem touched down at the Venice Film Festival on Tuesday for the competition world premiere of Oscar-winning French director Florian Zeller ’s highly anticipated thriller Bunker . Bardem plays an architect who takes on an ethically questionable project to build a survivalist bunker for a tech billionaire, in a move that will lead his wife (Cruz) of seventeen years to question their relationship. It marks the first time the stars who wed in 2010, and share two children together, have shared the big screen together in the role of a fictitious married couple. Related Stories News Casey Affleck On 'Company': "I Was Responding In Part To Raging Conflicts In The World, And To Things Inside Myself" -- Venice Documentary 'Musk' Review: World's Richest Man, And His Digital Avatar, Thrashed In Damning Alex Gibney Doc - Venice Film Festival The couple were asked at the press conference for the film whether they had put any of their real-life marriage into the roles, and whether they sometimes argued about work. Watch on Deadline “We are very good at really creating fiction and reality; otherwise, we won’t survive in this job,” replied Bardem. Cruz said it would be unimaginable that they had never argued once over the course of their 30-year relationship but that they rarely got heated over work. “We both really love this profession, but it’s true that there is a good balance in terms of how much you are speaking about work,” she said. “Obviously, if you are preparing a movie together, obviously that is going to be very present in the conversations. But we haven’t done this very often… it has appeared like every five years because all the things that we were offered, we didn’t think they were for us, or for us at that specific moment.” “But with this, there was no question because it was with Florian. When we had the first meeting with him about it, because we both loved the script, we knew that we were going to be protected.” Cruz suggested Zeller had a way of getting an actor to bring their life experiences to their performances, without bringing in their personal life. “Have somebody like him in the middle, you feel safer because you know there are going to be days that are more tricky, big arguments in the movie… emotional scenes… and I’m very grateful to Florian because he was always watching us, always feeling and seeing everything, without invading, he was a real protection for us in that way, and it was really beautiful to have that.” Zeller said he had approached the couple for the film simply because he “adored them” but also admitted he was intrigued as to how the fact they are a real couple would impact the film. “They are among the greatest actor actors working today, and so obviously it was an honor for me to work with them,” he said. “But I have to say that from the very beginning, I was also interested in having them together on screen, because I thought it would be a unique way to capture something special as a real couple, to give layers to all the scenes of this film, to blur the line, between reality and fiction, but to try to approach something that I’m interested in, which is the burning authenticity of the truth, and to do that for actors, you have to be very bold, you have to be very fearless and ambitious, and this is what they are, and that’s why they are such great artists.” Trump Admin Attacks UK Plan To Boost BBC Content On YouTube Apple TV & HBO Max Set Primetime Showdown After Early Wins; Winners List; More U.S. Summer Record In Play As Spidey No. 1; ‘Odyssey’ Wins Global Battle Surprise Movie ‘You Can See Everything’ Reviewed; More Pics In Focus Read More About: Comments

title: Javier Bardem Feels a “Responsibility” to Speak Out on Political Issues: “I Have You Guys Listening to Me”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 8, 2026 6:20am The 'Bunker' cast hit Venice Courtesy of Getty Naturally, real-life couple Penelope Cruz and Javier Bardem were immediately quizzed on how much their marriage spilled into Florian Zeller ‘s Venice competition feature, Bunker , at the movie’s press conference on Tuesday afternoon. Ahead of the movie’s red carpet premiere, Zeller, Bardem and Cruz were joined by co-stars Stephen Graham, Paul Dano and Patrick Schwarzenegger on the Lido to promote the film, following a renowned architect (Bardem) offered the chance to secretly design a survival bunker for a billionaire who is convinced that the end of the world is near. As he lets himself be seduced by this morally ambiguous project, his wife (Cruz) begins to question their marriage. Related Stories Movies Inside 'DAU,' the 20-Year Soviet Simulation That Became Cinema's Strangest Ghost Story Movies John Turturro "Grateful" to Zurich Film Festival for Golden Eye Award Honor Zeller confessed he was inspired to write the screenplay after reading an article about Meta tech billionaire Mark Zuckerberg building an underground bunker in Hawaii. “It was a secret project, meaning that everyone involved in this project had to sign an NDA, to make sure no one would know,” said the French filmmaker. “For some reason, the information went public, and I thought it was a fascinating paradox because this man who made a fortune based on the idea of connecting people together [through Facebook and Instagram], was working on a plan B to isolate himself from the rest of the world.” Questions around isolation, human connection and morality drive Bunker , as does an authentic wife-and-husband performance from the Spanish A-listers. Zeller said he coaxed the pair on board the project because he “adores” them, but also because he needed that legitimacy. “I think they are among the greatest actors working today, and so obviously it was an honor for me to work with them,” he continued. “But I have to say that from the very beginning, I was also interested into in having them together on screen, because I thought it would be a unique way to capture something special as a real couple — to give layers to all the scenes of this film, to blur the line, of course, between reality and fiction, but to try to approach something that I’m interested in, which is the burning authenticity of the truth.” He added: “To do that for actors, you have to be very bold, you have to be very fearless and ambitious, and this is what they are, and that’s why they are such great artists.” Bardem, who is particularly outspoken on a slew of political issues, including his support of Palestine, was asked during the presser about actors being told to “stay in your bunker, stay in your lane.” How important does he think it is to tell stories “outside of our own yard”? The Oscar-winning actor responded: “Well, I think as an artist, you have a responsibility to make a story happen and to tell the story that the director, the author, wants. And then you, as an individual — it doesn’t matter if you’re an artist, an actor, a plumber, or a taxi driver — you have the right to expose your truth or what you think is important.” He continued: “Obviously, I have more resources to do it than a taxi driver because I have this thing [gesturing to microphone] and I have you guys listening to me. So, the responsibility is a different one, and that’s what I think is important: to have a responsibility toward the world that we live in, and I don’t take it for granted.” He told the press conference that this movie speaks on those themes, especially “how much we are willing to see, feel, welcome [each] other” and “how much we are going to isolate ourselves and criminalize and dehumanize each other.” Cruz and Bardem were both probed on starring in Oscar-worthy films this year, Bardem’s The Beloved and Cruz’s Olivia Wilde hit The Invite , and conceded they were proud to represent their country on an international scale. But the Spanish actress also talked about being a woman in the industry and feeling pulled to intriguing female characters when reading a screenplay: “This woman says precisely the things that I usually think, and so I really wanted to be able to express these things and these feelings in public. This is why I wanted to be a part of this film,” she said. Cruz added that sometimes women “are used as puppets, and this is very sad.” She told the room: “There are few women who take very important decisions in the world, and I think this is a very sad reality. We are sort of manipulated, and I have to say that I’m usually quite optimistic. [But] when it comes to the role of women in the world, I am slightly worried. However, I do think that younger generations are realizing our importance, and so they’re starting to think this way, and they are opening their eyes. And maybe young people are more interested in politics now than they have ever been in the past.” Graham, Dano and Schwarzenegger weighed in on being a part of Zeller’s project, gushing over the filmmaker and his script. But the married Spaniards were the heroes of the presser, and even joked about arguing over their work: “No, no, never!” replied Bardem, prompting laughs from the room. Cruz chimed in: “I’ve known you for more than 30 years… Imagine if we never argued!” The 2026 Venice Film Festival runs through Sept. 12. THR

title: Penélope Cruz Says It Would Be ‘Very Contradictory’ to Star in ‘Bunker’ and Refuse to Talk About Politics: It ‘Involves So Many Aspects of Where the World Is Right Now’
full_text: Sep 8, 2026 6:17am PT Penélope Cruz Says It Would Be ‘Very Contradictory’ to Star in ‘Bunker’ and Refuse to Talk About Politics: It ‘Involves So Many Aspects of Where the World Is Right Now’ By Ellise Shafer , Rebecca Rubin Michael Buckner Penélope Cruz and Javier Bardem have proven that they aren’t afraid to speak out about politics, with the power couple being especially vocal about their support of Palestine. It was inevitable that the topic would come up at the Venice Film Festival press conference for their new film “ Bunker ,” which also doesn’t dance around timely issues. Directed by Florian Zeller, they star as a husband and wife whose 17-year marriage begins to unravel after Bardem’s character, an architect, agrees to build a survivalist bunker for a tech billionaire. Related Stories Wim Wenders Clarifies His Stance on Filmmakers' Role in Politics After Berlin Controversy: 'We Are the Opposite of Politicians ... We Are the Antidote' Asked about their choice to speak up about politics as actors, Cruz pointed out that it would be “very contradictory” not to do so while starring in a movie like “Bunker.” Popular on Variety “We don’t have to agree with our characters, we don’t have to agree sometimes with the story, but this involves so many aspects of where the world is right now — things that affect all of us, future generations,” Cruz said. “There are so many things in this film that it would be really contradictory to then be here and say, ‘Oh, I don’t wan to talk about that.’ It’s impossible. And that’s why a situation like [this press conference] is sometimes more scary than, I don’t know how many weeks of shooting that we did. But still, I don’t think it would make sense to say, ‘I don’t talk about politics.'” Bardem added that it “doesn’t matter if you’re an artist, an actor, a plumber, a taxi driver, you have the right to expose your truth on what you think is important.” “Obviously I have more resources to do it than a taxi driver, because I have this thing [the mic] and I have you guys listening to me. So the responsibility is a different one,” he continued. “And that’s what I think is important, to have a responsibility towards the world that we live in and I don’t take it for granted. But artistically speaking, this movie speaks about that, about how much we’re willing to see, feel, welcome the other, or fear based on what we imagine, our pre-judgments, our fears. Based on that, how much are we going to isolate and criminalize the other? And I don’t know the answer, but it’s a good question.” Zeller wrote and directed “Bunker,” which also stars Paul Dano, Patrick Schwarzenegger and Stephen Graham. The movie marks his return to Venice, where his prior film “The Son,” starring Hugh Jackman, competed for the Golden Lion in 2022. An acclaimed playwright, Zeller made his feature directorial debut with 2020’s “The Father,” which won Oscars for Anthony Hopkins and for adapted screenplay. The director has cited Stanley Kubrick’s “Eyes Wide Shut” as a key inspiration for “Bunker.” Like Kubrick, who cast then-married Tom Cruise and Nicole Kidman as partners on the verse of unraveling, Zeller described wanting to blend “fiction and reality” by spotlighting a real couple. Although Barden and Cruz have appeared in many movies together over the years, including “Jamón Jamón,” “Vicky Cristina Barcelona” and “Everybody Knows,” Zeller said he was intrigued that they had never played long-wed spouses. “I loved ‘Eyes Wide Shut,’ this ambivalent proposition presented to the audience where you’re not quite sure what you’re being invited to watch,” Zeller told Variety . “Is it fiction? Is it another version of fiction? Where is the line between reality and fiction? That permeability between reality and fiction seemed to me a truly fascinating project.” Asked about what it was like to work together on “Bunker” and if they ever argue about work, Bardem said they “are very good at either creating fiction or reality, otherwise we would not survive in this job.” He then joked, “And if we do argue? No, no never.” Cruz laughed and added, “I know you for more than 30 years, imagine if we’d never had an argument.” On a more sincere note, Cruz said: “We both really love this profession, but it’s true that there is a good balance in terms of how much you are speaking about work. Obviously if you are preparing a movie together, that is going to be very present in the conversations. But we haven’t done this very often. Naturally, it has appeared like, every five years.” Cruz continued that working with Zeller made them both feel comforted throughout the filming process. “We knew we were going to be protected in that way, in terms of having someone in the middle who is inviting you not to bring anything from your personal life, but you are going to bring yourself and everything you have experienced in your life,” she said. title: ’60 Minutes’ Gives A Peek At Story Lineup For Season Premiere Following Tumultuous Revamp
full_text: Skip to main content By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted Matt Gutman Dropped From Former ABC News Field Producer’s Wrongful Termination Lawsuit; Disney, ABC Remain As Defendants History Is Paramount: As The Last Warner Bros Merger Trial Proved, A Legal Victory Is No Guarantee Of A Happy Ending In Latest Threat Of Regulatory Retaliation, Donald Trump Says He’ll Report NBC News’ Kristen Welker To FCC For “Rebuke Or Punishment” View All September 8, 2026 6:16am Norah O'Donnell interviews Air Froce officer whose plane was shot down over Iran. The season premiere of 60 Minutes on Sunday will feature Norah O’Donnell’s interview with the the weapon systems officer whose plane was struck down in Iran, leading to a successful rescue operation. The newsmagazine will be starting its 59th season with plenty of scrutiny: It’s the first original broadcast since a tumultuous revamp earlier this year. The network ousted executive producer Tanya Simon and brought in Nick Bilton to succeed her, while correspondents Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega were dropped and, sharply criticizing the changes in an all-staff meeting with Bilton, Scott Pelley was fired. The three correspondents have all claimed political interference in their stories, something that the network has denied. Just Watch Our Show" Under CBS News editor in chief Bari Weiss , the show has brought in Ross Douthat, a former New York Times columnist, as a correspondent, and upped O’Donnell’s role on the broadcast. Those joining as contributors include Gianna Toboni, former senior correspondent at Vice News, who is also a CBS News national correspondent; Sebastian Junger; Ariel Levy, a staff writer at The New Yorker; and Trevor Phillips, who is also senior global affairs correspondent for the network. In the interview, the officer is identified by the call sign Dude Four Four Bravo. Another segment, from correspondent Jon Wertheim, will be a look at the Los Angeles Rams. title: How to Write Chad Powers: Go With “Your First, Stupidest Thought”
full_text: Skip to main content By Tony Maglio Plus Icon Tony Maglio View All September 8, 2026 6:09am Glen Powell in season two of 'Chad Powers.' Disney/Daniel Delgado Jr. Logo text Chad Powers ( Glen Powell ) should probably attend class a bit more. The Chad Powers title character is known around the Southern Georgia University campus for the “athlete” suffix of his student-athlete status. What I’m saying is he’s dumb — but in the most endearing possible way. That’s the way the Hulu comedy’s showrunner Michael Waldron ( Loki ) likes it. Waldron says the “most joyful stuff” to write in Chad Powers is the (prosthetically) masked man’s bizarre, roundabout answers to personal questions that could otherwise out Powers as Russ Holliday — or at least as not a real person. The exchanges that spark joy for Waldron do the same for viewers, and they’re not as difficult to write as you might think. Related Stories TV Meet Wynn Everett, the (Delightful) "Gus Fring" of 'Chad Powers' TV Taylor Frankie Paul Returning for 'The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives' Season 6 “That’s why I’m writing this show because, in some ways, it’s whatever your first stupidest thought. You don’t actually even have to be funny. The character is a real cheat because he just says stupid shit, and and the comedy comes from the great actor from how Glen sells it and then everybody’s reaction to it,” Waldron told The Hollywood Reporter . “I mean it is a precise thing and it’s like, ‘Well how stupid is it?’ It was fun this season to interrogate it a little bit. It’s like, as Russ says to Ricky, ‘Chad is stupid. I’m making deliberate creative choices.’ Now, I think that’s probably just [Chad] retroactively justifying a crappy performance.” “I could write Chad as a character forever,” he added. “I’ll be really sad to not get to write him.” With just six 30-minute episodes per season (by design), some of these idiotic run-on stories inevitably hit the cutting room floor. “In [the season two premiere ], there was a thing that we cut out where he’s in the trainer’s room when he gets brought back, and he’s— it’s so stupid,” Waldron said. “He’s talking about how he’s like having to manually beat his heart. How all of his automatic body processes are no longer automatic. So he says, like, ‘I’m controlling the individual enzymes in my gut.’ It’s just so self indulgent and stupid. So we cut it. But to watch Glen perform it on the day was hysterical.” Should Waldron and Powell get their way, and they probably will, Chad Powers will get one more season from Hulu. If season two is Russ/Chad in a Bruce Wayne/Batman parallel, as Waldron told his writing staff, season three, the College Football Playoffs, will explore more of a Peter Parker/Spider-Man duality. Those relationships are more different than they might first appear. “This season Russ is actually much more comfortable because he’s kind of had that catharsis at the end of the first season, where he’s like, ‘I’m happier as Chad,'” Waldron said. “The emotional arc of this season I would say is about him starting to take steps toward the idea of well, can you ever be okay being Russ again? That’s what Ricky is challenging him with, reminding him they’re the same guy.” That’s the DC Comics parallel from the Marvel writer. “In a third season… do you have to do Peter Parker and Spider-Man, where Chad has to say that Russ is part of his life in some way? Will we have to embrace that convention?” Waldron posed. “Maybe. We’ve always talked about that.” Tom Holland in Spiderman, Glen Powell as Russ Holliday on Chad Powers, and Robert Pattison as Bruce Wayne. Chuck Zlotnick/Columbia Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection; Disney/Daniel Delgado Jr.; Jonathan Olley/Warner Bros./Courtesy Everett Collection It is rare the co-creators of a series want said show to end after just 18 episodes, but that “was always the intent ” for Chad Powers , Powell told THR . “One of my pet peeves on TV is when people don’t stick the landing,” he continued. “When people draw things out. I’m like, ‘Come on!’ When you have a story that ends perfectly, it just makes me so happy.” For someone with roughly zero free time on his hands, the busy movie and TV star (and University of Texas student!) has given the Chad Powers timeline a ton of thought. “The lie” of Chad Powers the character could not possibly make it through an entire college football offseason, he realized pretty early on. “When you have the amount of eyeballs on this one man at the center of this team in South Georgia, as sort of the legend of Chad Powers grows, this lie becomes harder and harder to pull off in front of the world,” Powell said. “You want to honor that. It’s kind of the fun of the show.” So Waldron will be sad to no longer write Chad poorly tap-dancing around inquiries into his background, and whatever happens in the Natty (National Championship) — assuming we get that — the conclusion of Chad Powers will be bittersweet for fans. Powell asks you to trust the process. “We have a very exciting culmination in mind. So that’s the plan,” he said. “I’m really happy with where it’s all heading.” THR

title: Inside ‘DAU,’ the 20-Year Soviet Simulation That Became Cinema’s Strangest Ghost Story
full_text: × Skip to main content 'DAU' Ilya Khrzhanovsky On a cold night in November 2011, in a field outside Kharkiv in northeastern Ukraine, a gang of thugs stormed a Soviet scientific research institute, beat and humiliated the staff and burned the place to the ground. None of it was real. Well, some of it was. The institute was a film set — a working re-creation inspired by the Moscow institute run by the pioneering quantum physicist Lev Landau. It claimed, at the time, to be the largest set in European cinema history. Some of the thugs were actual neo-Nazis, led by real-life Russian fascist Maksim Martsinkevich, who would later be imprisoned for posting racist videos, investigated for murder and, in 2020, found dead in his cell of an apparent suicide. Related Stories Movies John Turturro "Grateful" to Zurich Film Festival for Golden Eye Award Honor Movies 'Musk' Review: Alex Gibney's Mammoth Elon Musk Doc Is a Poleaxing Portrait of the Tech Titan as a Con Man Given Way Too Much Power to Be Stopped Cameras rolled as the building burned. They continued to roll as the crew held a party on location, amid the ashes, with an open bar and music courtesy of electronic musicians Peaches and DJ Spooky. For three years before that night, the set had functioned less like a traditional backlot than a sealed micro-state. If you believe the rumors — and much of what is known about this project is only speculation — participants were required to wear authentic 1930s to 1960s-era clothing, right down to their underwear. They ate Soviet-style food, bought bread from the institute cafe with newly minted Soviet-era rubles and smoked Soviet cigarette brands. Anachronisms were banned: No mobile phones, no internet, no laptops. Women were reportedly forbidden to use modern tampons. All news came from a fully staffed on-set newspaper and radio station. The KGB officers were played, in some cases, by actual former KGB officers, and they could detain and interrogate other cast members. Not everything was filmed and recorded, but a lot was. Some 700 hours of footage, shot on 35mm film, and around 8,000 hours of recorded dialogue. None of that was the original plan, however. The initial idea, when a 29-year-old Russian director named Ilya Khrzhanovsky pitched it in 2006, was for a fairly conventional art house biopic of Landau — the recipient of the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physics, who was nicknamed “ Dau ” — financed by the European Union funding body Eurimages with German and Swedish support. What it became instead was Dau : a two-decade multimedia leviathan that has so far yielded more than a dozen experimental films, art installations in Paris and London, an aborted plan to rebuild the Berlin Wall, a ban in Russia for creating “pornographic propaganda,” accusations of abuse and exploitation, and a mythology so dense that the work itself all but disappeared behind it. ‘DAU’ Ilya Khrzhanovsky The Dau project became one of cinema’s great ghost stories. Akin to Orson Welles’ The Other Side of the Wind or Terry Gilliam’s The Man Who Killed Don Quixote — films that traded for decades on the mystique of never quite existing. For 20 years, the tales and whispers have circulated about the “mad Russian” director and his experiment. Some called it a “Stalinist Truman Show ” or “ Big Brother in period costume.” Some of the rumors, and a few of the reports at the time, paint Khrzhanovsky as a tyrant who went mad with power, like Colonel Kurtz in Heart of Darkness (or maybe Francis Ford Coppola making Apocalypse Now ). But Khrzhanovsky’s original idea, for an epic biopic on the life of Landau, never completely disappeared though. The filmmaker kept the footage he shot in Kharkiv between 2008 and 2011 — all 700 hours of it — and left it in a fridge for more than a decade. Now, 20 years later, the “mother film,” as Khrzhanovsky calls it, the biopic that spawned the leviathan, is finally finished. The 165-minute movie, titled simply DAU , premieres in competition at the Venice Film Festival this month. “[The new film] is more or less the model I wrote almost 20 years ago and that we filmed, starting from 2008,” Khrzhanovsky, now 51, explains via video call from Paris, where he’s completing postproduction with characteristic last-minute intensity. “[But] I didn’t really touch this movie from the moment when I finished the shoot [in 2011] until December 2023, when I started to edit and reorganize the material and find a new cinematic language for it.” Lev Landau makes for an unlikely epic hero, but his life offers up plenty of cinematic drama. A prodigy who started college at 14 and published major works on quantum theory before his 20th birthday, Landau worked with pioneering physicist Niels Bohr and, in 1937, was named head of the theoretical division of the secretive Institute for Physical Problems in Moscow. He was reportedly as experimental in his private life as in his physics, including practicing polyamory. At the height of the Soviet Terror, he was arrested for comparing Stalin to Hitler but dodged the Gulag. Rehabilitated, he worked on the project to build the Soviet atom bomb. In 1962, in the same year he became a Nobel Laureate, a crippling car crash left him bedridden until his death in Moscow in 1968. Compared with the other films to have emerged from the Dau shoot — the more experimental films DAU. Natasha and DAU. Degeneratsiya were screened at the Berlin Film Festival in 2020 — the mother film DAU promises to be almost mainstream: a Doctor Zhivago -style epic, albeit with discussions of quantum mechanics and a fair bit of explicit sex thrown in. It also arrives burdened by an entirely new scandal. Ahead of the festival, the Ukrainian government took the unprecedented step of formally complaining to Venice for selecting the film for competition . “At the time when Russia is continuing its war of aggression against Ukraine, systematically destroying cities, cultural heritage and national identity, offering one of the world’s most prestigious cultural platforms to a project linked to the Russian state and its networks of influence sends a deeply worrying signal,” reads the joint Aug. 17 statement from Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ministry of Culture and the Ukrainian embassy in Italy. The statement goes on to list the film’s alleged connections to Vladimir Putin’s Russia, including Khrzhanovsky’s Russian identity; and that of lead actor Teodor Currentzis, the Greek-Russian classical conductor who plays Dau in the film. There is also the connection to Sergei Adoniev, the Russian oligarch who bankrolled the original shoot, and who has been sanctioned by both Ukraine and the U.S. for his alleged ties to Putin. Khrzhanovsky took to Facebook on Aug. 20 to post a point-by-point rebuttal of the criticisms, noting that “ DAU is not an instrument of Russian state cultural policy. It is an artistic statement about the nature of totalitarian evil.” But speaking with The Hollywood Reporter, he says he understands the Ukrainian position. “The war is the war, and I cannot judge the position of Ukrainians who are suspicious of a Russian who spent time in Ukraine,” he says. “I wanted to correct the lies because things like saying I represent the Russian state is literally not true. I think it was misunderstanding and misinterpretation. But I don’t want to judge. They should do whatever they need to do to win this war.” The objection reflects how radically the perception of Khrzhanovsky’s Dau experiment has shifted over the course of two decades — from transcendent art project to exploitative scandal to, now, geopolitical lightning rod. The Stalinist Truman Show To understand the mythology of Dau , you have to go back to 2006. The year before, Khrzhanovsky had won a Tiger Award at Rotterdam for his first feature, the hallucinatory drama 4 . In that film, three strangers — a meat merchant, a prostitute and a piano tuner — meet up in an all-night bar in Moscow. They all invent fake biographies and spend the evening telling made-up stories from their imagined pasts. After they separate, these fantasy realities begin to dominate their everyday lives. Off the success of 4, Khrzhanovsky secured his European funding for what still looked like a straightforward Landau biopic. Everything changed when he met Adoniev and persuaded the Russian oligarch to bankroll the project. Adoniev had made his fortune in the mobile phone business; Forbes in 2017 estimated his wealth at $800 million. Freed from budgets, schedules and the ordinary logic of film financing, Dau the modest European art house movie mutated into a massive experiment designed to plunge participants — and, eventually, audiences — into the re-created horrors of the Stalin-era Soviet Union. The filmmaker’s own audit reveals the staggering numbers behind the project, listing “392,000 auditions, 40,000 costumes, 12,000- square-meter set, 10,000 extras, 400 principle roles. 700 hours of 35mm film, 8,000 hours of recorded dialogue, 500,000 set photographs.” ‘DAU’ includes massive set pieces not shown in the earlier movies, including a sequence involving “70 tons of cabbage.” Ilya Khrzhanovsky The project attracted remarkable participants beyond its massive cast of extras. Currentzis, the acclaimed classical conductor, agreed to play Dau after meeting Khrzhanovsky socially in Moscow in 2005. Performance artist Marina Abramović and opera director Peter Sellars took on roles. Real Nobel Prize-winning physicist David Gross and acclaimed mathematician Shing-Tung Yau took working residencies in Kharkiv, conducting real science in period costume. The idea behind the casting was to recruit to match the characters. So cleaners to play cleaners, academics to play scientists, even criminals and former KGB agents to play their Soviet equivalents. The Movie That Ate Itself In the three years of filming, only a handful of journalists were allowed inside “the institute.” Michael Idov spent several days there for a piece in GQ . He was allowed to move on and offset, given the official status of a “visiting foreign dignitary,” but required to dress in a three-piece suit and fedora and engage in period-appropriate small talk. In his 2011 piece, Idov described Khrzhanovsky as “unhinged,” portraying him as a dictatorial director who turned his set into an oppressive totalitarian microsociety. Actors were not just expected to perform but to physically experience life under the Soviet regime. “The real world was like a set to us,” Currentzis recalled in an interview with The Guardian in 2019. “We were sleeping and waking up and working in the clothes we had worn inside. When we were out, it was like visiting another time.” According to Currentzis, the reality of the Dau set was not always pleasant. “If the ‘KGB’ grabbed me, they could send me to jail. They could behave really badly to you,” he recalled. “I felt very uncomfortable many times, but it’s the same discomfort I feel in my own life. If we want to make something that is real, it has to be like real life.” Not everyone experienced it as art. Matthias Ganghofer, who worked as a first assistant cameraman on the Kharkiv shoot, would later stand up at a Berlin Film Festival press conference and say he found the experience on set “humiliating.” When he was caught using a cellphone, a violation of the project’s rules of historic authenticity, his name was marked on a blackboard for all to see. He claimed he left the project after three months. Khrzhanovsky says he fired him. “I fired a huge amount of people,” he adds. Speaking to THR , Khrzhanovsky speaks of the periods on set where there was no filming but life in the institute continued as a kind of “extended rehearsal.” He downplays the more extreme elements of the experience, noting that, for example, KGB arrests and interrogations were always agreed upon in advance. THR reached out to Currentzis, Ganghofer and several other members of the original Dau shoot for comment. Lol Crawley, one of the three cameraman on DAU , was not on the Kharkiv shoot, but he remembers a demanding but happy production, and a director who never resembled the tyrant of the rumors. “Ilya was in control, like any good director, but was such a warm and generous person to work with,” he says. (From L): Ilya Khrzhanovsky and cinematographer Jürgen Jürges instruct an actor on the set of ‘DAU’ Ilya Khrzhanovsky The GQ article was headlined “The Movie Set That Ate Itself.” But it didn’t. Eventually the money simply ran out — Khrzhanovsky estimates Adoniev spent around 25 million euros, about $40 million in today’s money, before pulling the plug — and the set burned in that staged massacre of November 2011. What survived was footage. Rather than cut one film from it, Khrzhanovsky began cutting many, along with a series of increasingly elaborate live installations built around the material. The first, in Paris in 2019, spread across the Théâtre du Châtelet and Théâtre de la Ville, immersing visitors in screening rooms, re-created Soviet interiors and hours of unseen footage. “I’m absolutely, 100 percent sure that what we’re experiencing here will be in the history books of Paris, of art history, of scientific innovation, of cinema history,” said Ruth Mackenzie, artistic director of Théâtre du Châtelet, of the 2019 Paris exhibition, describing the multi-site project as a once-in-a-generation “game-changer.” There was a plan to go further still, re-creating the Dau project in Berlin with an interactive exhibit that would have involved building a replica Berlin Wall in the German capital, creating a walled-in “city within a city.” Visitors would be required to purchase “visas” to enter and, once inside, it was promised, would experience life as it was in the old GDR. The project would end with a ritualistic tearing down of the wall on Nov. 9, 2018, 29 years to the day after the historic event in 1989. Chinese dissident artist Ai Weiwei was set to build the wall. Artists like Abramović and Run Lola Run director Tom Tykwer were involved. Brian Eno and Robert Del Naja of Massive Attack also signed up. “It’s the most extraordinary and multilayered art project I’ve ever heard of,” said Eno at the time. “You often hear things described as ‘ambitious.’ Nothing I’ve ever encountered comes close to the ambition of Dau .” It never happened. Berlin authorities objected on safety grounds to the project. There were also complaints from locals at the cost — reportedly close to $8 million — and the idea of using taxpayer money to re-create a dictatorship. There was talk of a “Disneyfication” of Stalinism. Over the years, bits and pieces of the Dau project have continued to emerge, in different forms. Last year, at the San Marco Art Centre in Venice from Sept. 5 to Nov. 23, Khrzhanovsky hosted the Dau exhibit The Quantum Effect , which featured footage shot in Kharkiv of scientists debating quantum and string theory. The Scandals Begin The first Dau films to emerge from the Kharkiv material, DAU. Natasha and DAU. Degeneratsiya — the former just over two hours, the latter more than six — screened at the Berlin Film Festival in 2020. DAU. Natasha , in competition, won a Silver Bear for outstanding artistic contribution for cinematographer Jürgen Jürges, the man responsible for most of those 700 hours of footage. Both films sparked an uproar. The controversy was hottest around DAU. Natasha . The film focuses on a cafeteria worker, played by Natalia Berezhnaya, and her colleague Olga (Olga Shkabarnya). They gossip, flirt with customers, and go out and get drunk. One evening after a roaring party, Natasha goes to bed with one of the institute scientists. She’s called in for questioning and torture by the KGB. The interrogation scene was the source of most of the controversy. Hatchet-faced officer Azhippo (played by Vladimir Azhippo, a former KGB officer) belittles and humiliates Natasha. In a particularly grim scene, he forces her to strip and insert a bottle into her vagina. Critics, assuming the scene wasn’t simulated, accused the production of sexual assault. ‘DAU. Natasha’ Courtesy of Phenomen film At the Berlin press conference, Khrzhanovsky was cagey and evasive when asked what in the film was “real” and what was staged for the camera. But the actors all supported him. Everyone on set, Berezhnaya told reporters, was “in charge of our own senses and emotions. We were well aware of what we were doing.” She denied the rape charges unequivocally. Cinematographer Jürges agreed. “In those scenes, we always had a safety vow. If somebody did not want to go along, we could stop at any time,” he says. “We didn’t work according to a screenplay; we were living our lives,” says Berezhnaya, though she reminds everyone that “we have amazing directors and amazing editors, and we are amazing actors.” That didn’t stop the outrage. A letter, published on now-defunct Russian feminist film website KKBBD.com and signed by five Berlinale-accredited Russian journalists, called out the festival for including, in the wake of #MeToo, a film that “contains scenes of real psychological and physical violence against nonprofessional actors.” Khrzhanovsky finds the allegations, particularly that of actual sexual assault, patently absurd. “[Berezhnaya] said it, she repeated it, and you can see it, if you just understand anything about anatomy, you see it isn’t real. But that story was there and got repeated and repeated,” he says. “Of course, it was an unusual way of filming, and having people play characters close to themselves [helped] them go further emotionally. But the whole time, you are on a set with a cameraman, a focus puller, a boom operator.” Berezhnaya was nominated for a European Film Award for best actress, but the controversy around the movie meant “she couldn’t celebrate, couldn’t be celebrated,” according to Khrzhanovsky. “Monica Bellucci came up to her and said what an incredible performance it was,” he recalls, but such praise was drowned out by scandal. Russia banned the film as “pornographic propaganda,” while Western press largely dismissed it. Then COVID struck, and the film barely saw a release. Looking back, it’s striking how the Dau films shown in Berlin were viewed through the lens of the #MeToo movement that had transformed Hollywood and cultural discourse. Stories that might once have been framed as the excesses of an avant-garde visionary — actors staying in character for months on end, living in Soviet-era quarters in period costume — now appeared as potential acts of exploitation and misuse of power. Interesting, too, how the project’s warnings about Russian totalitarianism, particularly stark in DAU. Degeneratsiya , and its discussions of art, philosophy, religion and quantum physics were largely overlooked at the time. Now, the “mother film” DAU arrives with yet another interpretive framing: that of current Ukrainian politics. The Political Context The protests against DAU by the Ukrainian government ahead of this year’s Venice Film Festival highlight a dramatic shift in geopolitics, one that makes the project’s original context almost unrecognizable. All the filming for DAU in Ukraine took place between 2008 and 2011, more than a decade before Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion. At that time, Russian-Ukrainian cultural collaborations were not only common but actively encouraged, with co-productions regularly receiving support from both countries’ film funding bodies. Adoniev, the project’s main private funder, left the project years before he was sanctioned by Ukraine in 2022, and later by the U.S. in 2023, for his ties to Putin. “When we started to make this project, it was a completely different reality,” Khrzhanovsky notes. “Russian-Ukraine co-productions were everywhere. People would move from here to there. It was a completely different reality.” Khrzhanovsky’s own position vis-à-vis Russia has shifted just as dramatically. He has renounced his Russian citizenship in protest of the invasion of Ukraine, and holds British, German and Israeli passports. He set up the XZ Foundation with journalist Mikhail Zygar to counter Russian propaganda, mocking Putin’s description of the invasion as a “special operation.” As a result, he has been labeled a “foreign agent,” a designation used to target critics of the Putin regime. In Russia, Andrei Lugovoi, a member of the Duma and a former KGB agent, has called him a “master traitor” and accused him of “sabotage against Russia.” The Ukrainian objections also focused on Currentzis, who lives and works in Russia as artistic director of the Perm State Opera and Ballet Theatre. He took Russian citizenship in 2014 and has never publicly denounced Putin’s war on Ukraine — factors that make him particularly controversial in the current climate. “However one may judge his decision not to make such statements [against the war], judging a person on the basis of the citizenship they hold — and, even more so, using citizenship acquired years after most of the filming as evidence of the film’s current connection to the Russian state — is not justified,” Khrzhanovsky wrote in his Facebook post. Speaking to the political turmoil around the film, the director takes the long view. “Right now there is an emotional reaction mixed in with a need to protest the war, which I understand,” he says. “They need to stop the war, and if they want to destroy monuments, or forbid certain storytellers, that’s not my business.” History, he suggests, has a way of changing the narrative. “My Jewish mum was born in Ukraine and grew up there,” Khrzhanovsky says. “She was a Holocaust survivor and then moved to Uzbekistan, went back to Ukraine, then Moscow, and then Israel. Now she lives in Berlin. I grew up in the Soviet time when, in the movies about the Second World War, we didn’t say ‘Nazis,’ it was always ‘Germans.’ Now I hold a German passport. My mum too.” “I believe soon we will see a more multidimensional picture of who we are, what we did, and what kind of world we live in,” he muses. “That was part of my task with this project — to create this picture, to create this model.” Dau Phenomen Berlin Return of the Mother Film Khrzhanovsky returned to the “mother film” three years ago, going back into the editing suite with funding from Germany, France and Sweden, plus Rotterdam’s Hubert Bals Fund. Adoniev’s involvement with Dau , he says, ended in 2019. He still had the original material, and the original idea — Lev Landau and the Soviet Union from the 1930s through the 1960s — but his take on it had changed. “[Returning to] the material, the way I describe it, is like cognac. The cask is time,” he explains. “The style of the movie, its language, how I edited it, has changed because of the 20 years in between.” Of course, he adds with a smirk, “a 20-year cognac could still be a shitty one.” Ilya’s original idea of making a biographical film about Lev Landau had already changed after he cast Currentzis in the lead. His quantum physicist became Greek and his story started to diverge from Landau’s biography. The entire second half of the new film, Khrzhanovsky says, has “no connection whatsoever” to the life of the real Landau. DAU is structured in three parts, each shot by a different cinematographer, representing different periods of Landau’s life. Revisiting the footage, Khrzhanovsky realized he had assembled, back in 2008, a team that would go on to define contemporary art cinema: veteran German cinematographer Jürgen Jürges, best known for his work with Rainer Werner Fassbinder, in Kharkiv and Moscow; the then-up-and-coming Brit Lol Crawley, later an Oscar winner for The Brutalist , in Saint Petersburg; and Manuel Alberto Claro, who would go on to shoot Melancholia and Nymphomaniac for Lars von Trier, in Kharkiv. Crawley, the first cinematographer to shoot on the project, says the design was deliberate from the start: “Three different cinematographers, three different production designers, three different looks for the three different sections of the film,” Crawley tells THR . What he mostly remembers is the scale — “incredibly ambitious,” he says — and “these amazingly complex handheld sequences, where we had to reset and reset over and over again.” All 700 hours of 35mm footage were kept in climate-controlled storage — “many years in Switzerland, then moved it” to a “fridge in Berlin.” It was all Fuji 400, a stock the company discontinued in 2010, which should have made the pickups he needed in 2023 impossible. But Khrzhanovsky had anticipated that. Fuji agreed to produce the stock for one more year “just for us, just for Jürges,” he says. “I took that remaining stock and put it in the fridge with the rest of the 700 hours.” In 2024, he took out the reels and shot his additional scenes. “We filmed everything, down to the last meter.” The aged stock had lost two stops of sensitivity, meaning the image on the old film was substantially darker, which had to be compensated for with additional lighting. Khrzhanovsky refuses to disclose which scenes come from the original shoot and which are the add-ons. Khrzhanovsky, if you haven’t realized by now, is an obsessive. Dau hasn’t made him rich — he’s racked up huge debts, not least for storage — or particularly famous. He’s been called an abuser, a pornographer, a dictator and an agent of the Russian state. But he can’t let Dau go. The Quantum Artist In some ways, Khrzhanovsky was born for this. He comes from a film family — his father, Andrey, was an acclaimed director whose 1968 animated short, The Glass Harmonica , has the distinction of being the first animated movie banned in the U.S.S.R. (The film depicts a bleak, gray city controlled by greedy, corrupt authorities. Censors felt this was a bit too close to the reality of the ’60s Soviet Union.) Khrzhanovsky’s godfather was Soviet screenwriter and dramatist Sergei Yermolinsky, who was imprisoned and then sentenced to internal exile in Kazakhstan for “anti-Soviet activities” for offenses, including his friendship with dissident novelist Mikhail Bulgakov, and only freeed after iconic Soviet director Sergei Eisenstein ( Battleship Potemkin , Ivan the Terrible ) successfully petitioned for his release. For Khrzhanovsky, the Soviet past he re-created in DAU is “part of my DNA.” Returning to the story of Landau, the physicist whose experiments changed our notion of the reality of time and space, felt, he says, like he was creating a “quantum picture” — where multiple realities — past, present and possible future — exist simultaneously. “I started thinking about the me who began thinking of the project 20 years ago,” he says. “Then there are the real 20 years of my life, and of the lives of all the characters, the actors,” Khrzhanovsky reflects. “My life and the life of other characters are also part of the story of this process.” The whole Dau project, he says, “is much bigger than me,” but the film DAU , “this fictional story about society, about the relations between people,” he says, “belongs to me. I’m the author of this film.” Khrzhanovsky’s “mother film” is clearly a different beast from his other Dau features. It’s more conventionally structured, more obviously cinematic. It includes massive set pieces not shown in the earlier movies: a hypnotic sequence of women on an assembly line, smashing up an endless stream of clay rabbits; huge crowds in period costume crossing a re-created St. Isaac’s Square in St. Petersburg/Leningrad; a gigantic Soviet propeller plane trudging across a vast field; piles and piles of rotten cabbages — Khrzhanovsky has said he used 70 tons for the single scene. Crawley remembers one such sequence vividly: following Currentzis, as Dau, through the streets of Saint Petersburg carrying a red balloon, before he emerges into a square filled with dogs and fish, trams crashing, soldiers pouring out and destroying paintings and artworks. “It was incredibly ambitious,” he says. Khrzhanovsky still wrestles with the mythology surrounding the Dau project. The reports and rumors, the endless stream of shifting scandals, have developed their own momentum, often overshadowing the actual work. “That’s why I prefer to talk about this new movie, not the Dau project or the other films, and not about this or that rumor,” he says. “Just discussing or denying these things leads them to repeat and repeat. All the work gets dissolved in the lake of rumors.” If the “mother film” DAU , so obviously a work of cinema and not a “Stalinist Truman Show ,” had been the first work released, he admits, “the whole conversation would have been different.” But he says he cannot look back or be concerned about how he or his films will be judged in the current historical moment. He knows too well how quickly that moment can change. “The historical perception is always changing,” he says. “We see it with Israel. I hold an Israeli passport, and I still have the Israel flag on my Facebook. But I know what Israel is doing in Gaza and the West Bank. My son [the journalist and activist known as Andrey X] is one of the most influential bloggers on the West Bank, fighting with the state of Israel. That’s what I mean about a quantum picture.” Whether Venice audiences will embrace this “quantum approach” to narrative remains to be seen. The film demands patience. “It’s not an easy movie. It’s not easy to watch. It’s long. It’s mostly in Russian language,” says Khrzhanovsky. “And it’s a complex story, but I think there are still a lot of people around the world who may be interested in watching this movie.” The Feast That Never Ends Khrzhanovsky insists he won’t be “doing Dau for the rest of my life.” But he is also, at present, still doing Dau . Eight Dau films are available on his bespoke VOD platform, dau.com, with five more listed as “upcoming releases.” Many share the same characters and the same events, approached from different angles. DAU. New Man follows an institute experiment to engineer “perfect soldiers” by weeding weakness and empathy out of the new Soviet man. DAU. Sasha Valera is a May-October love story between two of the institute’s janitors. That is the logic of the whole enterprise: 14 features to date (including the “mother film”), plus the installations and exhibitions — Khrzhanovsky mentions the possibility of a Dau book or books — all from a three-year shoot in Kharkiv. One set of events recut again and again into parallel worlds. This is what is meant by a “quantum project”, the same material suspended in several states at once, resolving only when somebody finally looks at it. For 20 years, almost nobody has. DAU has existed as rumor rather than reality, scandal rather than art, shelved alongside cinema’s great ghost stories. Other movie ghosts, Gilliam’s The Man Who Killed Don Quixote or Welles’ The Other Side of the Wind , eventually surfaced – in forms no one quite expected. In Venice, on Sept. 7, so will DAU . THR

title: John Turturro “Grateful” to Zurich Film Festival for Golden Eye Award Honor
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 8, 2026 6:00am John Turturro Primož Korošec John Turturro will be honored with the Golden Eye Award at this year’s Zurich Film Festival . The Emmy-winning U.S. star is being recognized for his performance in Noah Segan’s The Only Living Pickpocket in New York , a project that is already garnering awards buzz . In the film, Turturro plays Harry, a seasoned pickpocket whose carefully controlled life is thrown into turmoil when a job goes wrong, setting off a tense chain of events that unfolds over the course of 36 hours. Turturro will accept the award in person at the Swiss film festival on Sep. 26, and share insights into his colorful acting and filmmaking career during a Zurich Film Festival Masters session the following day. Related Stories Movies 'Musk': Alex Gibney Shares His Take on Elon Musk's "Global Right-Wing Agenda" and the "Almost Existential Fear" of Talking He Encountered: Venice Movies Laura Poitras and Rachel Lauren Mueller on Making ICE Doc 'They're Here' Like a "Horror Movie" “I am grateful to the Zurich Film Festival for this honor,” said the actor. “I was immediately drawn to Noah’s script and to the world he created in The Only Living Pickpocket in New York . There’s a sense of tension as the clock works against Harry, balanced by a finely drawn character-driven story set in a particular time and place in New York. As a lifelong New Yorker, the world felt rich and evocative, and there was a delicacy about it that felt almost radical about the story Noah was telling,” he added. Turturro’s career spans four decades, having worked with acclaimed directors such as Spike Lee, the Coen brothers, Martin Scorsese, Robert Redford, Robert De Niro, Nanni Moretti and Pedro Almodóvar. He first gained international recognition through his collaborations with Lee, appearing in Do the Right Thing and Jungle Fever . With Joel and Ethan Coen, he acted in Miller’s Crossing , Barton Fink , O Brother, Where Art Thou? and The Big Lebowksi , in which Turturro created the iconic Jesus Quintana. For his lead performance in Barton Fink , he won best actor at the 1991 Cannes Film Festival. Other credits include The Truce , Quiz Show , The Color of Money , The Good Shepherd , The Room Next Door and The Batman . On television, Turturro is best known for roles in Monk , for which he won an Emmy, as well as The Night Of , Mr & Mrs Smith and Severance . He received the Camera D’Or Award at the Cannes Film Festival for Mac , in 1992. Other films as a writer and director include Illuminata , Romance & Cigarettes , Passione and Fading Gigolo . CEO of Zurich Film Fest Christian Jungen said Turturro carries The Only Living Pickpocket in New York from the first minute to the last, “while also turning it into a deeply personal love letter to his hometown.” He continued: “Even though he portrays the antihero, we find ourselves rooting for him right until the end. That’s exactly what John Turturro is characterized by: he creates characters that are exaggerated for the screen yet feel completely true to life at the same time. With the Golden Eye Award, we honor an actor who has left his unmistakable signature on cinema for decades.” The Golden Eye Award honors actors and actresses who shape the current cinematic year while also ranking among the most significant performers of their generation. Previous recipients of the award include Jude Law, Kristen Stewart, Dakota Johnson, Jake Gyllenhaal, and Benedict Cumberbatch. Julianne Moore is set to receive Zurich’s Golden Icon Award this year. title: Carly Rae Jepsen Could’ve Been a One-Hit Wonder or a Mainstream Megastar. Instead, She Became Far More Interesting
full_text: × Skip to main content Carly Rae Jepsen was photographed July 29 at PMC Studios in Los Angeles. Styling by Sophie Hardeman. Open24hrs vintage Jean Paul Gaultier top; vintage silk garter belt; Greta Garmel skirt; her own jewelry. Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion; Hair: Summy Layo; Makeup: Pircilla Pae It’s early afternoon in West Los Angeles and Carly Rae Jepsen is a kid again. Dressed in a delicate sheer skirt with bright green socks popping under stiletto heels for her Hollywood Reporter photo shoot, she turns to her stylist to politely verify that she can get her loaned shoes dirty. The millisecond she gets that go-ahead, Jepsen’s jumping into a tree on the deck of The Hollywood Reporter ‘s headquarters, red hair streaming as she adjusts and mugs for the camera. Her tendency to throw herself into creative endeavors without overthinking has made her the artist she is today, allowing her to sidestep the pitfalls of one-hit-wonderdom. Jepsen shot to fame nearly 15 years ago at the age of 26 when her song “Call Me Maybe” became an early exemplar of modern virality. Living under a rock would hardly have prevented you from hearing the ubiquitous monster hit — and replaying it in your head ad nauseam. (You’re hearing it now, aren’t you?) Related Stories Movies Liam and Noel Gallagher Lock Arms at Venice Premiere of 'Oasis: Don't Look Back in Anger' Movies Gallagher Brothers Skip Venice Press Conference for Concert Doc Now, 40 years old and just months after the birth of her first child, Jepsen has arrived at a place few might have predicted back then: neither a Taylor Swift-level megastar nor fading into obscurity by limply chasing another pop smash. “Where I’ve landed now in my career is the sweet spot,” the singer tells THR . “I can live a life, go to the grocery store, have a family, tour music that I love and have an audience,” she says. “That’s a very hard-earned, balanced thing that we’ve had to work at.” Initially released in 2011, “Call Me Maybe” became a global sensation in 2012, earning her two Grammy nominations and a spot atop the Billboard Hot 100. “In the moment, it was all happening rather fast,” Jepsen says. Her career moves after skyrocketing to success were less strategic than instinctual, she says: “If I’m being honest, I felt a little voice from inside screaming at me to hold on to why I started.” Her longtime friend and collaborator Tavish Crowe, who co-wrote the breakout song, was there to remind her that “Call Me Maybe” was just a “flavor” of Jepsen’s range as a singer. “I’ve always been blown away by how deep she can go on a song,” he says. “She’s always pushing the needle of what someone might expect or doing things that feel like they haven’t been done before.” With the hit song came a difficult period of adjustment and self-reflection. “It was so overnight that I feel like I understand what it must be like for some people who live in that space consistently, and my heart goes out to them,” Jepsen says. Maybe some celebrities feel they’re better at managing sudden success, she muses: “I’m just not very good at it.” Fame didn’t just happen to her, it happened to everyone in her orbit. But her main way of processing what happened back then is to simply think back and reflect. “I’m giving shit away, but I don’t care,” she says. “On a future song, that’s coming out after this album… There’s a song called ’16 and Rising.’ [It’s] about my coffee shop days and a guy I was dating back then, and what happened as I moved through this,” Jepsen says. “[It’s about] why I couldn’t quite settle for this beautiful life that was ahead of me because I was pining for something that I didn’t quite know what it was.” Greta Garmel top; The Frankie Shop skirt; vintage shoes. Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Since the release of her breakthrough album, Kiss , Jepsen has kept one foot in the door of mainstream pop success and another in a more avant-garde space. Jepsen’s latest release, Day and Night, is a feat of balance, a double album that reflects the yin-yang equilibrium she’s striven for throughout her post-“Maybe” career. It’s divided thematically into Day, filled with sun-soaked psychedelic pop anthems, and Night, dripping in synth-heavy electropop. Jepsen hadn’t set out to make a bifurcated album; as with many of her most ambitious projects, it grew organically out of a back-and-forth with Crowe. She was heading on a trip to New York and was planning to show him the music she’d been working on. “He and I share music kind of like brother and sister in a very deep way,” she explains. Jepsen presented her friend one song from Day and one song from Night, and he suggested they think of them as contrasting material for a single project rather than two separate albums, as she’d originally imagined. She continued to mull the concept back home in L.A. until one day, driving around the city (once again with Crowe), the idea of Day and Night came to her. “As we were listening to stuff, it just felt like a song would naturally slot itself into the Night section or the Day section,” Crowe says. “Even before they were fully produced, too, you could still tell.” In the beginning, there were many pushes to divide the songs into two albums, but Jepsen says she “passionately disagreed” with that idea. “I wanted them together. They felt like two sides of the same thing,” says Jepsen. The duality of the album mirrored Jepsen’s own upbringing. “I grew up in two different houses because my parents divorced when I was quite young and remarried to incredible stepparents,” she says. It was a “very modern idea of co-parenting,” where she and her brother would switch houses every two days, both within 10 minutes of each other in the town of Mission, British Columbia. Her parents, all four of them, would have monthly meetings to discuss rules for the children. But the houses were very different. Night and day, you might say. “My mom’s a little bit more free spirit, hippie-ish, and my dad’s a little bit more the opposite of that,” she says. “I feel like musically there was a connection. They all love James Taylor, they all love Joni Mitchell, but they also had different flavors in terms of what my stepparents brought to the table with their musical tastes.” That duality made its way into Jepsen’s live shows, a mix of hits old and new. She considers it a win that “Call Me Maybe” isn’t the focal point of her concerts anymore, slotted within the set instead of as the closer. “I don’t think it’s a place to sit and hold resentment — what a useless waste of energy,” she says of the obligation to play the song she’s best known for. “If it’s a calling card that makes a couple of people happy, it’s not really about me anymore.” Left: Vintage bicycle tee; Kimberly Corday skirt; vintage hosiery; Prada shoes. Right: Open24hrs vintage Jean Paul Gaultier top; vintage silk garter belt; Greta Garmel skirt; her own jewelry. Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion (2) After the whirlwind release of “Call Me Maybe” and Kiss , Jepsen took a break and headed to Broadway. She’d spend her nights doing Rodgers and Hammerstein’s Cinderella , while her days were occupied by her follow-up album, 2015’s Emotion , which would become a critical success. In the clearest indication of her abiding cultural clout, the video for the album’s biggest single, the bouncy earworm “I Really Like You,” featured an ebullient, fully committed Tom Hanks and included a cameo by Justin Bieber. The album solidified Jepsen as much more than a one-note artist, pushing the boundaries of what mainstream pop could be with risky sonic choices. She didn’t know whether it would be what her legion of fans wanted and, to an extent, didn’t care. In hindsight, she’s thankful for her “obliviousness” to the mechanics of fame and believes she was better off for her relative cluelessness about how to handle it. Among her most naive assumptions, she says, was that she would continue writing her own material. “Around that time, the idea of you being a pop writer for your own project was sort of like, it was cute,” she explains. “I had to learn how to know who my people were.” In another possible sign of her ingenuousness, Jepsen has maintained the same label and team at Interscope for her entire career, something of a rarity in the music industry. She counts herself lucky, gushing about the “incredible relationships” she’s had with her A&R. But she did make notable changes in her management. “I’ve had some good experiences with people, and I’ve had hard ones too,” she says. “It’s taken a second to figure out the right team for my management, and now I’m happier than I’ve ever been.” To anyone who has followed her career, it’s hard not to wonder whether “the hard ones” is a reference to Scooter Braun, the high-profile former manager and music executive who signed her in the wake of “Call Me Maybe.” There has been plenty of speculation about the circumstances in which they parted ways — as there has been with several other former Braun clients — but Jepsen claims to hold no ill will toward him. Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion “I knew that I was on a different journey than he understood,” Jepsen says. “I wanted to do something a little bit less mainstream, and I liked what he had offered, but I didn’t necessarily think it was what I wanted anymore. I felt like it was just going to be a little bit easier to shake hands, walk away and go let my freak flag fly, so to speak.” The singer didn’t leave empty-handed, however. “I took one of his employees with me,” she admits, cheekily. Jepsen feels more freedom to explore with her current managers and says Interscope has always done well by her. “I wouldn’t say I had complete agency from the beginning, but not because they were trying to take it away,” she explains. “But I didn’t know how to take it.” The broad, extensive rollout that Interscope is giving Day and Night is a clear indication that the label trusts Jepsen’s instincts. The album is a collaborative mashup of all her “favorite people,” as well as newcomers introduced through friends. One of those newcomers is playwright, actor and social butterfly Jeremy O. Harris, who directed the music video for one of the album’s prerelease singles, “Don’t Leave Me on the Dance Floor,” starring Alden Ehrenreich. Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion “She’s such an artist,” Harris says. “She understands her audience and her own work incredibly well but is also excited for someone who can show her another lens.” People are lining up to work with Jepsen. Fellow Canadian treasure Jacob Tierney shared that he’d been eager to get Jepsen to write an original song for the first season of his hit hockey romance series Heated Rivalry , but it wasn’t in the budget. Jepsen hasn’t heard from him yet about the second season but admits that writing a song for it would be a “dream” for her. “It was an incredible show. Ilya is the name of my son. Maybe, not maybe because of that show,” she says, referring to the character played by Connor Storrie. Perhaps the most significant collaboration on Day and Night has little to do with the music. The album was made against the backdrop of one of the most transitional times in Jepsen’s personal life. While making Day and Night , she was falling in love with the man who would become her husband, musician Cole M.G.N., one of her collaborators and a producer on the album. Later in the process, as the album was being mixed, she became pregnant with their son. When it’s suggested in our interview that the album has effectively served as a time capsule for this time in her life, she asks, “Can I steal that?” “I don’t want to say that my album’s only sunshine and rainbows and happiness because if I’ve done my job right, there’s some depth to it,” she says. But she’s not going to lie about how she’s feeling: “I’m the happiest I’ve ever been.” Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion This story appeared in the Sept. 9 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

The Emmy award-winning actor-writer-director will be feted for his performance in The Only Living Pickpocket in New York , written and directed by Noah Segan. Turturro will touch down in Zurich to accept the award in person on September 26 and will also participate in a Zurich Film Festival Masters session on September 27. In The Only Living Pickpocket in New York , Turturro stars as Harry, a seasoned pickpocket whose carefully controlled life is thrown into turmoil when a job goes wrong, setting off a tense chain of events that unfolds over the course of 36 hours. Set against the streets of New York, the film combines the momentum and suspense of a crime thriller with a character-driven story about a man confronting the choices that have shaped his life. Related Stories News Julianne Moore To Receive Zurich's Golden Icon Award Festivals Zurich Bolsters Position As Awards Circuit Stop-Off As 'Bunker', 'Club Kid' & 'Adult Supervision' Join Gala Lineup Turturro’s career spans more than four decades, working with a range of filmmakers such as Spike Lee, Joel and Ethan Coen, Martin Scorsese, Robert Redford, Robert De Niro, Nanni Moretti and Pedro Almodóvar. His breakthrough roles in Lee’s films Do the Right Thing and Jungle Fever firmly established him as a distinctive actor of his generation. Watch on Deadline Turturro has been a frequent collaborator with the Coen brothers, appearing in films such as Miller’s Crossing , Barton Fink , O Brother, Where Art Thou? and The Big Lebowski , in which he created the iconic character Jesus Quintana. For his lead performance in Barton Fink , he won the Best Actor Award at the 1991 Cannes Film Festival and the David di Donatello Award. Further credits include Francesco Rosi’s The Truce , Redford’s Quiz Show , Scorsese’s The Color of Money and Di Niro’s The Good Shepherd as well as Almodóvar’s The Room Next Door , Matt Reeves The Batman , Mr. Deeds , Anger Management and Transformers He later reprised his role as Quintana in The Jesus Rolls , which he wrote, directed and starred in. Turturro received the Camera D’Or Award at the Cannes Film Festival for Mac , his directorial debut. His other films as a writer and director include Illuminata , Romance & Cigarettes , Passione and Fading Gigolo . His TV work has seen him earn an Emmy for his guest appearance on Monk and he was nominated for an Emmy, Golden Globe and SAG Award for his performance as criminal attorney John Stone in HBO’s The Night Of . Further TV credits include The Plot Against America , Mr. & Mrs. Smith and Severance , the latter of which he received Primetime Emmy nominations for both seasons. Yesterday, ZFF announced that it would also be honoring Zurich-born actress Elisabeth Baume-Schneider with a Golden Eye Award, making her the youngest actress to receive the award. Baume-Schneider is featured in two films at this year’s festival – Eurotrash and animated film De Rägebogefisch . The 22 nd Zurich Film Festival takes place September 24 – October 4, 2026.
