title: Casey Affleck On ‘Company’: “I Was Responding In Part To Raging Conflicts In The World, And To Things Inside Myself” — Venice
full_text: Skip to main content By Andreas Wiseman Andreas Wiseman Executive Editor, Film & International @AndreasWiseman More Stories By Andreas ‘Company’: First Footage Revealed For Casey Affleck’s Venice Drama Featuring His Two Sons Telluride’s Surprise Movie Sparks Industry Guessing Game As Studio Buyer Emerges; Update With A Winner — The Dish Venice Film Festival Chief Alberto Barbera On Oscar Chances, Why Gaza Doc ‘NAZA’ Is Playing So Late & Why He’s Confident U.S. Studios Will Return View All September 8, 2026 5:41am Indiana Affleck, Emily Alyn Lind, Scoot McNairy, Casey Affleck, Adelaide Clemens, Nick Nolte and Caylee Cowan at the "Company" photocall at The 83rd Venice International Film Festival on September 08, 2026 in Venice, Italy. Getty Casey Affleck ‘s Venice Film Festival Competition drama Company is launching on the Lido today. Affleck was flanked at the film’s press conference by Adelaide Clemens, Scoot McNairy, Emily Alyn Lind, actress-producer Caylee Cowan — Affleck’s partner — and 85 year-old screen legend Nick Nolte. Affleck told the assembled journalists that actor Ben Mendelsohn, who also stars in the film, had arrived with the team in Venice but had to return home to be with his father who is unwell. The film also introduces Affleck’s son Atticus for the first time on screen and marks the second feature for his son Indiana. Both were seated in the front row but Affleck said he wanted to play ‘father’ and not have them exposed to questions today. Watch on Deadline Related Stories Reviews Venice Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline's Reviews News Ellen Burstyn Talks Future Direction Of U.S. As She Receives Venice Career Award: "I Pray My Country Finds Its White Line" Described as “a meditation on grief, vengeance, forgiveness, and the quiet acts of compassion that can heal even the deepest wounds”, the gothic drama is set over a single night in 1975 when a wintry holiday gathering is interrupted by a mysterious woman who recounts a tale from decades before. Oscar winner Affleck responded to a question about whether the film was an expression of anger about global conflicts: “It’s not explicitly a political movie. But I’m not impervious to the to the world around me, so I was responding in part to all of the sort of raging conflicts in the world, and to things inside myself. And what do we do with the the stuff in our life? All of us, not just me or someone over there or people living next door to me, but everyone, with the injuries and insults that we experience, the harm that has caused us, the pain and suffering, the injustice that we feel that makes us so angry and want to lash out and fight back. Is there another way to process those feelings? Is there another way? And and there’s no answer that’s given. I was I was just exploring those those questions.” He continued: “Chekhov said that art isn’t supposed to provide answers. It’s just supposed to formulate the problem. The metaphor he used was that the courts are there to formulate the problem, and the jury solves it. And I think the same is true for for art and for movies. What we’re doing is sort of formulating the problem. We’re not trying to to solve it or even really suggest a solution.” One journalist lamented to Affleck that it had been years since she had last seen him at the Venice Film Festival with Manchester By The Sea [Affleck was last at the festival in 2022 with Dreamin’ Wild ], and she wanted to know why he hadn’t been back since and what he had learnt about himself in that time: “Let’s see”, he responded. “I’m 51, so I was 41, and my kids grew up, and I went through COVID and divorce and a million things, and I took all of that stuff…You know, the good thing about being an artist, the best thing maybe, is that you can take all of the hardest experiences in your life and put it into your work, and it just makes you better if you’re willing to face it all, be honest about it all, and show vulnerably with those feelings, and allow for the fact that you might not be able to really fully understand them, but you’re willing to put them into what you’re making.” He continued: “It’s a blessing, and for me, it’s the only way that I can understand what’s happening in my own life. Sometimes I’ll see movies from five years ago and I think, ‘Oh wow, that’s what that was about. I had no idea. I didn’t know that is what I was going through at that time. That is what was on my mind.’ Because we go through our lives thinking about picking the kids up or making lunch or buying the groceries, but there’s this other stuff that’s churning deep, deep, deep down, and that’s the stuff that comes out when you’re making something. And then there you see it on the screen. You think, ‘oh, I guess that’s me’. So I think someday I’ll look back on this movie and I’ll say, ‘that’s me, and I’ll have a better understanding of what the last 10 years have been like.’ Unsaid was also the challenging period following the movie I’m Still Here , which led to Affleck having to settle two lawsuits out of court, and his name being pulled into the MeToo debate. He pulled out of presenting an Oscar at the 2018 ceremony and hasn’t been nominated by the Academy since his win for Manchester By The Sea in 2016. Affleck was asked at one stage why he cast his kids in his new film and whether he had to drag them “kicking and screaming” to do it: “That’s not inaccurate,” he explained. “Neither one of them really wanted to be a part of this production. I think that they grew up around it and had some interest in it and a sort of innate understanding of what it was, like I did. My dad worked in the theater for many years, and so it’s passed down, I suppose, which is a really nice thing, and they were willing to be a part of this. The casting process was pretty conventional. We just hired a great casting director, Avy Kaufman, who I’ve worked with before, but I couldn’t find people. I was sitting around the house doing read throughs of this script over and over, and and I would have my two kids read the younger and older teens, and and they were fantastic. I got to the point where I was there in pre-production and they were willing to show up and do it…they were amazing and it made it the best professional experience of my life by far because I got to go to work every day with my kids and hang around and I would do it over and over again if I could. I don’t think that they will let me but I I’m gonna try.” The multi-hyphenate was also asked why the film was dedicated to his parents. He explained that he had lost both parents this year and didn’t get a chance to show it to them, which he had wanted to do. Affleck went on to say that Venice was his favorite place to show movies and that being a part of the Venice launch of The Assassination Of Jesse James was probably his favorite festival experience. The full synopsis for the movie reads: “On a winter night in 1975, a mysterious woman named Evelyn arrives uninvited at a holiday gathering and tells the story of Tom, an aging hermit who rescues a stranded actress during a Colorado blizzard in 1953. To pass the night, the actress recounts an older tale of a farming couple who take in a troubled young drifter as a series of grisly murders spreads fear across the frontier.” Affleck co-wrote the script with Ron Hansen. Producers include Steven Schneider and Roy Lee via Spooky Features, Catherine Caylee Cowan, Dan Lawler, Affleck, Sean Patrick O’Reilly, K. Asher Levin, Enzo Marc, and Anthony Katagas. Executive producers include Ben Ross via Image Nation Studios, Rami Yasin for Spooky Pictures, Ronnie Exley and Jeremy Ross via Rabbits Black, Ron McLeod, Dr. Terence Chan, Brian Meng, and Maria Breese for 3:33 Creative Productions, and Jonathan Miller. title: Omaha Pulls Off a Star-Studded Hollywood Heist for the ‘Manningcast’ Schedule Release (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 8, 2026 5:35am 'Manningcast: Heist' Omaha Productions The Manning brothers may have pulled off their biggest heist yet. Sure, that’s the theme of this year’s Manningcast schedule release from Omaha Productions : An Ocean’s 11-style heist film, culminating in the reveal of the games they will be calling this coming season (including the Super Bowl), but the biggest heist of all may be what the former NFL stars pulled off onscreen in a 15-minute short film unveiling the schedule. The film, titled Manningcast: Heist , features some 40 cameos, spanning A-list movie stars to current and former NFL stars, and even a starring role by the NFL commissioner Roger Goodell himself. The result is high-energy, surprising and funny, with stars like Anne Hathaway, Jon Hamm, Paul Rudd, Larry David and Jason and Travis Kelce securing unexpected roles for themselves. Related Stories THR + Sportico: The Sports Issue Padel Spanks Pickleball: Inside the Rise of the New Celebrity Sports Obsession TV When and Where to Watch F1 Italian Grand Prix at Monza Watch: “The tone of the heist is sort of a larger metaphor for the show itself,” says Omaha Productions president Jamie Horowitz, in an interview with The Hollywood Reporter . “The Manningcast is meant to be a safe space, a show where everybody can just come on and talk about a love of football. And you may have heard this before, but Omaha has very pure brand values — we try to uplift and unify — and we hope you see that in everything we do. And we also hope that people feel those values in that piece. This video is trying to be just a joyride of fun.” According to Therese Andrews, the head of production at Omaha, planning for the reveal started in late 2024, and they began production in early 2025 at the Pro Bowl, where they could secure the first round of cameos. “We map out the cameo roles early on when we do the script, thinking about what kind of people we want, and then we chip away throughout the entirety of the year to see how to build into that,” Andrews says, crediting Omaha writer and producer DJ Gallo with building out the heist concept. “The process with the creative is both scripted and it’s also sort of improv as we go. So as we book certain people, we’re reshaping the creative based on who we think is gettable, who might be interested in it, and then we rework every time we film with somebody.” Omaha executives credit the Manningcast itself as being a helpful piece of that puzzle. In fact, they see the over-the-top promotion of the NFL altcast as serving as a virtuous circle. “I think part of the reason that Paul Rudd, Kevin Hart, or David Letterman appears on the Manningcast is because we do things like this,” Horowitz says. “If the Manningcast was just a football show, Peyton and Eli probably could still recruit lots of great people. But the more you see these types of projects from Omaha outside of Monday night, the more likely creative people want to be part of our little world.” ESPN surely doesn’t mind if Omaha goes hard on promotion either, especially with the sports media giant’s first Super Bowl coming at the end of this season. The result is a piece of content (a promo video no less!) that levels up their ambitions and brings a whole host of stars along for the ride. “The Mannings work the same way they played football; they’re just always sort of eye on the prize of what’s the next play, and how do we evolve and figure out how to make things bigger,” says Andrews. “That’s part of our process throughout the whole journey. As much as this is about the Manningcast , it’s really a collection of talent, and finding a way to make something that’s dynamic and fun for people to watch and just celebrate the fact that football is coming back.” THR

title: AMC Global Media Settles ‘Walking Dead’ Profit Participation Lawsuit for $120 Million
full_text: Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 8, 2026 5:22am Andrew Lincoln as Rick Grimes in 'The Walking Dead.' Jackson Lee Davis/AMC Logo text The Walking Dead lawsuit saga may finally be over. AMC Global Media said Tuesday that it had settled the lawsuit brought by Walking Dead creator Robert Kirkman and the show’s other producers, including Glen Mazzara, David Alpert, Charles Eglee and Gale Anne Hurd. The lawsuit, initially filed in 2022, was about the profit participation rights for the original Walking Dead series, and its first spinoff series Fear the Walking Dead . AMC says that it will pay $120 million to resolve the lawsuit, including $85 million this month, with another $35 million next year. Related Stories TV Netflix and AMC Global Media Ink $500 Million 'Walking Dead' Streaming Deal TV Jack Quaid to Voice Gravitator in 'Invincible' Animated Series The $35 million will also serve as an advance against future profit participation rights. The settlement was reached on Friday, Sep. 4. The Walking Dead is the most successful franchise in AMC’s history (the company just inked a $500 million streaming deal with Netflix for the franchise in July), and the company has been battling lawsuits related to it since 2013, when Frank Darabont and CAA filed a profits suit about the program back in 2013. Darabont and CAA’s suit was settled in 2021 for $200 million, but it helped spark the new challenge from the franchise’s other producers, who filed the lawsuit now being settled in 2022. At issue in the suit is how the company calculates and collects profits for the franchise, and in turn how much the show’s creatives would be owed. “Robert Kirkman, Robert Kirkman, Inc., Gale Anne Hurd, Valhalla Entertainment, Inc., David Alpert, Circle of Confusion Productions LLC, New Circle of Confusion Productions, Inc., Charles Eglee, United Bongo Drum, Inc., Glen Mazzara and 44 Strong Productions, Inc., on the one hand, and AMC Global Media, on the other hand, are pleased to announce the amicable resolution of all their remaining claims and litigation related to The Walking Dead television franchise,” the two sides said in a statement Tuesday. “The parties look forward to sharing in the continued success of the franchise for many years to come.” THR

We Are the Antidote' “Our acquisition strategy is driven by a desire to work with independent producers and creators who bring distinctive voices and fresh perspectives, says Hanna Mouchez, CEO of MIAM! Distribution. “Through these three projects, we explore themes that are central to our editorial vision: identity and belonging, diversity and representation, and the confidence to find your own place in the world.” Popular on Variety Sevens Inspired by the real-life journey of French international rugby player (and co-creator of the series) Séraphine Okemba, “ Sevens ” is a 13×22-minutes character-driven kids’ series celebrating female sport, powered by Girelle Production. As Rose, an average middle-school girl, decides to launch a female rugby sports team at her school, she and the girls joining her begin to build powerful bonds of friendship, solidarity and sisterhood. “Rugby is a sport built on values,” adds Okemba. “Within a team, players learn solidarity, mutual support and trust in yourself and others. They learn to trust themselves, and to trust others.” This collective adventure is the heart of “Sevens,” centering on how sport can empower young people, build confidence, proving that strength, courage and leadership have no gender. Currently in development with France Télévisions, with an expected delivery by the end of 2028, the show is co-directed by Guillaume Lorin, award-winning director of the TV special “Vanille,” and Vinnie Ann Bose, director of the César-nominated short “Suliamani.” Queerstory A bold young adults 20×6-minutes doc series bringing forgotten queer myths to the spotlight, “ Queerstory ” blends humor, documented historical sources and experts’ takes to share queer tales whose voices have too often been erased from history. From the truth behind Thor’s hammer and the goddess Amaterasu to Princess Badoure from One Thousand and One Nights, the show restores these legends to their rightful place in our collective memory. Driven by the distinctive voice of its creator Iris Miské and blending rough-edged graphic design with bold pop-culture references, the series combines sharp pacing, clever punchlines and compelling storytelling, inviting a broad audience to rediscover history through fresh, inclusive perspectives. “Queer people have always existed, all around the world,” hammers Miské. “In these times where LGBTQIA+ identities are globally threatened, ‘Queerstory’ builds a bridge between the past and the present, giving life to our queer ancestors, and arguments to fight bigotry.” The series will be delivered in May 2027 by Hauteville Productions and is set to premiere on Slash, France Télévisions’ digital platform dedicated to young adults audiences. Dad&Me A 52-minute coming-of-age TV special produced by Have a Nice Day Films and Les Astronautes, “Dad & Me” follows Alyona and her father Fiodor as they leave their Russian village to settle in Paris. On her very first day at school, Alyona cannot understand a single word of French, making friendship seem impossible. But when a rap competition unexpectedly brings her together with two classmates, she gradually finds her place between two cultures and discovers a new way to express herself. With her father by her side, every challenge can become an adventure. “Whatever your age, you always need courage to build a new life in a new country, town, or even neighborhood,” recalls director Olesya Shchukina who adapts her own childhood story with this special. ” “I wanted to talk about this experience and its complexity, so both kids and adults could relate.” Currently in production, “Dad & Me” is supported by a broad alliance of French funds, including Pictanovo, CICLIC, Région Sud, Procirep, France’s CNC National Film Board and French distributor Les Films du Préau. title: Longstanding Franchises, Distinctive New IPs Help French Animation Industry Weather Market Slowdown
full_text: Sep 8, 2026 5:12am PT Longstanding Franchises, Distinctive New IPs Help French Animation Industry Weather Market Slowdown Family-viewing, IP branch-out and bold creative-driven endeavors power Xilam, Mediawan Kids & Family and the whole French animation sector at Unifrance Rendez-Vous. By Kevin Giraud Plus Icon Kevin Giraud Latest MIAM! Distribution Expands Slate, Strengthens Partnerships With French Indie Producers, Unveiled at Unifrance Rendez-Vous (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago Female-Driven, Premium Period Dramas Spearhead Latest French Fiction Revolution 1 day ago Cartoon Forum Unveils Tribute Nominees, Introduces New Sustainability Award Ahead of 2026 Edition 6 days ago See All From left to right: 'Witch Detectives,' 'Chickies,' 'Astro Boy Reboot,' 'Submarine Jim'. Credits Mediawan Kids & Family, Xilam Animation Of the numerous formats impacted by budget cuts and labor shortage in the entertainment industry, animation ranks high in that rather bleak list. Yet for French production companies, distributors and sales agent who are gathering at the Unifrance Rendez-vous in Normandy’s Le Havre, hope is still a word with 24 animated fps. For Mediawan Kids & Family global partnerships and new business director Marie Lassalle, there’s strength in unity. “Sure, the market is pushing the entire sector to be more selective and to diversify its models (international co-productions, multiple financing sources, earlier consideration of rights and distribution channels as well as a greater focus on formats and production costs), but the answer can’t be solely economic. French creatives must continue to focus on their strengths, expertise, and the uniqueness of their universes.” Related Stories Wim Wenders Clarifies His Stance on Filmmakers' Role in Politics After Berlin Controversy: 'We Are the Opposite of Politicians ... We Are the Antidote' ‘Witch Detectives’ Credits Mediawan Kids & Family To Lassalle’s point, Mediawan brings “Witch Detectives” to the Rendez-Vous. A high-end, 26 half-hour episode 3D-series featuring three inseparable BFF trainee witches, the show is a pan-European new IP, co-produced by Method Animation (part of Mediawan Group) and Toonz Media Group with TF1, Super RTL, BBC and Rai already on board. A perfect illustration on how strong international partnerships can power ambitious projects, all the while retaining their French flavor. Popular on Variety For Xilam Animation , the answer to the current shifts comes from both legacy franchises (“Zig & Sharko” and “Oggy and the Cockroaches” have both sold worldwide) and strong original new IPs, such as preschool hit “Piggy Builders” and the laugh-out-loud comedy series “Submarine Jim,” headlining Xilam’s slate at the Rendez-Vous. “We’re also looking forward to launching our spin-off series ‘Chickies’ at the market,” adds Safaa Benazzouz, EVP Distribution at Xilam. “Derivated from our hit YouTube series ‘Where’s Chicky,’ which has reached reached billions of views thanks to our extensive, digital-driven distribution strategy. Today, making a digital hit requires both linear and digital exposure. But even if preschool is, to my opinion, the most competitive area, animation is ranking high in the total consumption on YouTube and streaming platforms, so there’s no shortage of demand.” Lassalle also identifies family viewing as a very significant trend. “Content that brings children and parents together meets a genuine demand from the audience, and often has a long lifespan. At Mediawan, we therefore look for projects with multiple layers of interpretation, accessible to younger audiences while also engaging the whole family.” While Xilam prefers still to target settled demographics (preschool, kids, YA) on both linear and non-linear programming, Benazzouz acknowledges the ongoing nostalgia trend for content from the 1980/90s that adults love to watch again, sometimes with their kids. “It does create a cross-generational viewing experience for the whole family, and this should be considered when producing animated series today.” The “Astro Boy” reboot, arriving in 2027 on Mediawan’s catalog and produced by Method Animation, and Shibuya International along with Tezuka Productions, is a particularly representative IP in this regard. According to Lassalle, it will introduce this iconic universe to a new generation, while also appealing to parents who grew up with the character. “In our distribution catalog, ‘Ulysses 31’ also illustrates the enduring power of these worlds that continue to resonate with multiple generations.” Beyond these well-known, solid legacy IPs, new concepts are also on the radar of both executives. “We look for concepts that are easy to identify, yet rich enough to last,” explains Lassalle. “Projects with a strong world, well-developed characters, and a compelling narrative.” The ability to make them travel easily while maintaining their unique creative vision is also key. With Madbox, Mediawan is currently developing “Pocket Champs” (a French video game IP with 72 million players) into a transmedia franchise designed to grow with its community, with a YouTube-first launch in 2027. “Digital development and the ability to leverage IP for new uses will be crucial in the near future,” she adds. “YouTube hits like ‘ Miraculous Chibi’ demonstrate the power of short formats designed for global platforms. For us, the challenge is to have a balanced catalog capable of appealing to diverse audiences, uses, and distribution models.” Credits Xilam Animation The same goes for Xilam. Over the years, the company grew its production studios to cover all animation techniques from 2D hand-drawn to full CG animation capabilities. “In terms of sales, we need and want to have a strong variety of formats and techniques,” underlines Benazzouz. “Which in turn allows us to have at least one programme in each category to present for every client. High-quality production, matched with character-driven new IPs with original design and strong humour, is what makes our programming really stand out.” Remaining agile while maintaining high editorial and production standards seems to be the answer to navigating these shifting tides. And both companies are hungry for more, as they head to the Rendez-vous, with Mipcom just around the corner. “Our integrated model, from development to production and distribution, allows us to support projects over the long term and fully realize their international potential,” concludes Lassalle. “And the recent launch of Wonderland Junior TV is a concrete example of that strategy: We are creating a free, reliable, and family-friendly destination in the U.S., which enhances the visibility of premium European content to new audiences.” With more than 1,700 episodes, Wonderland Junior TV is not only Mediawan’s own effort. Major European partners are on board as well, including Xilam, pushing French high-end, unique animation series beyond its borders. title: ‘Musk’ Review: Alex Gibney’s Definitive Documentary Puts the Pieces of Elon Musk Together — It’s a Lacerating Portrait of Technocratic Brilliance, Power Lust and Crackpot Delusion
full_text: Sep 8, 2026 5:05am PT ‘Musk’ Review: Alex Gibney’s Definitive Documentary Puts the Pieces of Elon Musk Together — It’s a Lacerating Portrait of Technocratic Brilliance, Power Lust and Crackpot Delusion Once you start lining up Musk’s scandals and cut corners, you see that he’s a creator of mirages who promises more than he delivers. By Owen Gleiberman Plus Icon Owen Gleiberman Chief Film Critic @OwenGleiberman Latest ‘Musk’ Review: Alex Gibney’s Definitive Documentary Puts the Pieces of Elon Musk Together — It’s a Lacerating Portrait of Technocratic Brilliance, Power Lust and Crackpot Delusion 1 hour ago ‘You Can See Everything’ Review: Nathan Fielder’s Documentary About Elizabeth Holmes Is a Shameless, Fascinating, Reality-TV-Eats-Its-Tail Look at Entitled Duplicity 1 day ago ‘The Debut’ Review: Julianne Moore Is Astonishing in Jesse Eisenberg’s Funny and Dizzying Community-Theater Comedy 2 days ago See All Courtesy of Venice Film Festival When a subject has been as exhaustively covered — and as infamous — as Elon Musk , the electric-car-entrepreneur-turned-rocket-man-turned-richest-billionaire-in-the-universe-turned-Twitter-disruptor-turned-DOGE-destroyer-turned-God-only-knows-what-he’ll-do-next, reviews of a documentary about him tend to lead by plucking out the film’s incendiary bits of investigative reportage, the ones that feel worthy of a news headline. “ Musk ,” Alex Gibney ’s 3-hour-and-45-minute documentary about the tech bro who would be king, has a handful of those. Related Stories Wim Wenders Clarifies His Stance on Filmmakers' Role in Politics After Berlin Controversy: 'We Are the Opposite of Politicians ... We Are the Antidote' The biggest revelation, to me, was the film’s detailed history of Musk’s attempt to put a self-driving car on the market — a technology that’s sure to be here at some point, though Musk, in his race to be first, was far too eager to announce that it had already happened. Tesla released its Autopilot driver-assist system in 2015 (and then the Full Self-Driving Beta program in 2020), marketing the new technology with ads that exaggerated the car’s powers. And so people were suckered. From the outset, there were accidents. More than 60 fatalities have been linked to Tesla’s driver-assistance systems. Talk about something that could put a dent in your image! But Musk, for the most part, succeeded in hushing up the lawsuits, the federal investigations, and the fatal crashes, which were evidence of a recklessness that should have given the whole world pause. Popular on Variety There are other places where Gibney colors in sides of Elon Musk you knew in a cursory way. It’s well-known that Musk has fathered many children — at least 14, though the people around him say it’s many more. He believes his progeny to be part of a larger war against population decline. The documentary, which features a highly illuminating interview with his ex Ashley St. Clair, goes into the details of how Musk, apart from his two spouses, would zero in on young women he thought would make good “breeders” and get them pregnant, dropping all interest in them after the babies were born. (They were required to sign NDAs.) The film also goes into details of his alleged drug use (ketamine, Ecstasy, psychedelic mushrooms). Yet what makes “Musk” such a lacerating and important watch, grounded in Alex Gibney’s supremely insightful but user-friendly mastery of the documentary form, is that it takes this flamboyant and in many ways elusive figure, with his tech ambitions and cosmic dreams and malignant megalomania, and puts him together, letting us see how one chapter of his life led to the next, and how the Musk dream wasn’t always so grandiose. You can see it evolve right along with his look. In the mid-’90s, at his first company, the relatively modest Zip2 (which essentially put the yellow pages onto the Internet), he looks just like the tech geek he was inside, skinny and unthreatening, with receding hair and a rabbity grin. But it’s not long before his Ayn Rand ambitions start to poke through. The hair fills in, the body thickens, and the smile gets elevated into a kind of aggro leer, as Musk makes himself over into his version of a tech-head Nietzschean superman. Gibney plays around a bit, creating a synthetic “interview” with Musk (who, of course, wouldn’t cooperate with him) by putting verbatim quotes of his into the mouth of an AI Elon. Late in the movie, when Musk is wreaking the havoc of DOGE, we see him killing off bureaucrats as if in a first-person-shooter video game. From the start, Musk has three obsessions: the Internet, energy, and space exploration. He first tried to purchase old Russian ICBM rockets (minus the nukes they were built to carry) for $3 to $5 million, and Gibney shows a fitting admiration for the innovation of Musk’s space dreams. He was leading a movement that was organic: the privatization of space exploration, which resulted from the U.S. government having lost all passion for it. The thrill was gone — for NASA, and maybe for the public. But Musk rekindled that (working in cooperation with President Obama). Sending up rockets was his original and driving obsession. Musk thought of himself as an engineer-magician in the mold of Steve Jobs. With SpaceX, even Musk’s failures (i.e., the first three launches) were spectacular. But he might have gone bankrupt if the fourth launch hadn’t connected. In a way, you could say that the first semi-scandal of Musk’s career was the way he took over Tesla, a sports-car company co-founded by Martin Eberhard in 2003, and then erased Eberhard out of the narrative of the company. Instead, it would all be his, with Musk showcased as the sole visionary — the Henry Ford — of the electric-vehicle revolution. His genius was marketing the Tesla as less a car than a shiny new tech gizmo on wheels. Yet this required a lot of smoke and mirrors, like the Tesla battery fraud: the claim, sold in advertisements, that you could just swap a new battery into a Tesla (it would be as easy as replacing two double-AAs!), when in fact the Tesla battery weighed 1,000 pounds. What Musk was selling was pure fiction. When people started having problems with the cars, Musk established a boiler room full of scammers who took the calls and lied about how the cars could be fixed. In essence, he was gaslighting his customers. The second scandal, according to the movie, is the way he gaslit his first wife, Justine Wilson (who is also interviewed), after their first child died of SIDS-related causes. “Musk” opens on something that’s not new ( I wrote about it five years ago ), namely Musk’s ardent belief in simulation theory — the notion that we are all very possibly living in a giant simulation, an idea bolstered for Musk by his love of video games, which became more and more sophisticated in their creation of simulated realities. The way he saw it: Who’s to say that we’re not all just part of a digital dream landscape, and that there isn’t some cosmic force out there playing us? While it doesn’t spend a lot of time on this idea, “Musk” uses it make a point: that anyone who truly believes this — and thinks it’s the higher wisdom — may not be in complete possession of his marbles. It’s not that Musk is less than brilliant. It’s that it’s his very brilliance that leads him to invest in the idea that his fruitiest fantasies are reality — like the one he began to evolve out of SpaceX that said we were on the verge of colonizing Mars. There was no truth to it. But Musk, like his future frenemy Donald Trump, was starting to think that he had the power to create his own reality. Once you start piecing together Musk’s scandals and cut corners and slipshod management, you see that he’s a creator of mirages who promises more than he delivers. There’s no question that the Tesla, as he finally designed it, is a strong and beautiful car, and that Musk’s early advocacy of electric vehicles was a positive force in the world. But his rocket program is increasingly mired in a kind of sci-fi stasis. (His fixation on Mars is right out of the cheesy ’50s.) And when Musk took over Twitter, which he had to borrow so much to buy that he wound up slashing the company to ribbons, it was a lesson in atrocious management (which he camouflaged as a testament to free speech), and he then applied that experience — as if it were a positive prototype — to his slashing of the government under Trump. He was out to make destruction look cool. Increasingly, though, his ventures began to seem like they were about little more than Elon’s simulated glory. Musk, as the documentary makes clear, is a genuine if flawed technocratic visionary, a messianic opportunist, and something of a crackpot. Around the time he was given a cameo in “Iron Man 2,” he’d begun to think of himself as a Tony Stark figure: a superhero right out of the comics. He used his Starlink satellite technology to influence the war in Ukraine (not necessarily in a good way), and he became a mega-donor and collaborator of Trump’s, in no small part, to squash the federal investigation into the Tesla Auto-Drive fraud. In doing so, he demonstrated that tech fascism doesn’t need to be a form of government; it can do an end run around government to control people’s lives by reducing them to cogs. That, “Musk” argues, is the world Elon Musk has been building up to, not intentionally at first, but once he got a taste of power. The film says that what should scare us about him is how he coddles his own interests by passing them off as the world’s. ‘Musk’ Review: Alex Gibney’s Definitive Documentary Puts the Pieces of Elon Musk Together — It’s a Lacerating Portrait of Technocratic Brilliance, Power Lust and Crackpot Delusion Reviewed at Bleecker Street Screening Room, New York (Venice Film Festival, Out of Competition), Aug. 31, 2026. title: ‘Musk’ Review: Alex Gibney’s Mammoth Elon Musk Doc Is a Poleaxing Portrait of the Tech Titan as a Con Man Given Way Too Much Power to Be Stopped
full_text: × Skip to main content By David Rooney Plus Icon David Rooney Chief Film Critic DavidCRooney1 Follow Sign Up View All September 8, 2026 5:05am 'Musk' Courtesy of the Venice Film Festival Not long after news first emerged three years ago that Alex Gibney had begun work on an in-depth study of Elon Musk , the uber-tech bro went on the defensive on his social media platform, Twitter. Sorry, I mean X. “It’s a hit piece,” he cried, before switching to the totally mature “Gibney is a douche.” It must have been no surprise to the filmmaker that his subject would decline to make himself available for Musk , a whopping documentary think piece running close to four hours, which traces in dense detail the dizzying ascent to stratospheric wealth and influence of the man who dreams of colonizing Mars. Related Stories Movies Laura Poitras and Rachel Lauren Mueller on Making ICE Doc 'They're Here' Like a "Horror Movie" Movies Venice Home Crowd Gives Italian Horror 'The Spiral' 9-Minute Standing Ovation Gibney’s solution to that key absence turns out to be a stroke of creative genius. After having his team pull together a data base with every statement Musk had ever made and every interview he had ever given, the director’s digital effects crew set about developing a CG avatar to address the camera as if in a sit-down chat from a gaming chair, sticking strictly to the billionaire business mogul’s own words. Musk The Bottom Line A provocative combo of indignation and alarm. Venue : Venice Film Festival (Out of Competition) Release date : Friday, Oct. 16 Director : Alex Gibney Screenwriters : Alex Gibney, Michael J. Palmer 3 hours 45 minutes What could be more appropriate for a subject who has hypothesized that we could all be living in a computer-generated base reality, a simulation controlled by some future power, as if all of humanity might be player characters in a video game? Gibney digs into the extent to which Musk’s ambitions were shaped early on by vintage sci-fi movies and books, though many have pointed out that he seemed to miss the anti-capitalist satire of one of his key inspirations, Douglas Adams’ The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy , instead treating it like a manual for technological advancement at any cost. This is the man who wants to ensure the survival of human civilization while our own planet teeters toward the abyss? If you buy that, Gibney seems to suggest, he has a bridge in Brooklyn to sell you. The filmmaker has likened his perspective in this project to that of Dorothy’s dog Toto in The Wizard of Oz , alert to the shuffling feet beneath the curtain rather than being bamboozled by the shyster title character’s techno showmanship. With a clarity that makes his conclusions hard to refute and a wealth of visual material, spiffy graphics and insightful interviews to keep it interesting throughout the epic run time, Gibney pulls back the curtain, charting the path of the South African whiz kid, who grew up under apartheid and has never denounced the racially discriminatory regime. The film hopscotches from Musk’s first U.S. software company, Zip2 — the sale of which netted him $22 million despite the enterprise never having turned an operational profit — through the key business ventures that helped consolidate his power and multiply his net worth. Those steppingstones include the purchase of Twitter, which soon cratered in value but became a crucial bullhorn to legitimize his partly illusory personal narrative for a devoted cult, sweeping the stated goal of promoting free speech under the rug. This was a logical extension of what Musk’s first wife, Justine Wilson, considers his strategic gaslighting skills, allowing him to shape exactly the image he sought to project, not of an investor but of a visionary inventor. That’s why it was so important to Musk to be credited as the founder of Tesla , which would come as news to engineers Martin Eberhard and Marc Tarpenning. Gibney paints Musk as an unabashed megalomaniac. He ventures outside the professional sphere to touch on the “legions of children,” as someone describes them; the disposable “breeders”; the drug use; and the father who seems like a nightmarish piece of work. But the gossipy tidbits almost pale next to the eye-opening shadiness of some of the business strategies. The Tesla chapter is compelling less for the success of launching electric vehicles on the market than the more inconvenient factors that somehow went ignored — from falsehoods about the time required to swap out a battery pack to the playing down of fatalities that resulted from glitches in self-driving cars, reported to have caused at least 65 deaths. Around the same time, Musk mastered the art of stock manipulation, as well as securing government handouts and energy credits. He’s now inextricably linked with Republican Party politics and more specifically Donald Trump. But the film notes that although foundational funding for Musk’s SpaceX rocket program came from the George W. Bush administration, along with a $1.6 billion contract that reportedly rescued the division from looming bankruptcy, it was the Obama administration that honored and expanded on the initiative through NASA. In retrospect, that now looks like an uncharacteristically laissez-faire decision. Gibney lays out the shift by which Musk turned away from the Democrats to align himself for personal gain with Trump, in what many believe was a case of him buying the 2024 election, funneling close to $300 million into the campaign. That opened the door to the infamous DOGE purge. Musk unleashed a team of 19-to-22-year-old Silicon Valley bros to kneecap government agencies of which they had zero understanding. But crucially, they did understand those agencies’ IT systems, giving them access to classified programs and Americans’ personal information. Some of the tech reporters interviewed maintain that all that data has been used to link pension funds and 401ks to SpaceX, creating a precarious balance. While the formation of DOGE, during which Musk bounced around the Oval Office like a kid in a candy store, was positioned as a cost-cutting measure and an assault on fraud and waste, by decimating the IRS, the department substantially increased the federal deficit. DOGE’s primary achievement now appears to have been hobbling government agencies to block all investigations of Musk’s companies. While the entire section of Gibney’s film on DOGE has the sobering effect of a corruption exposé and the fear factor of a ‘70s conspiracy thriller, the cruelest part of it all is the dismantling of USAID, the independent government department for international development founded by JFK in 1961. It’s estimated that 14 million lives in developing countries will be lost because of DOGE cuts, 4.5 million of them kids under 5. “USAID is a criminal organization,” Musk says at one point. “Time for it to die.” His stunt with “the chainsaw for bureaucracy” now looks like the most juvenile theatrics, especially given that hundreds of federal workers had to be rehired when their departments stopped functioning, in some cases receiving back-pay for the interim months. One of the most sinister examples of cause and effect in this culling is the immediate suspension, after Trump signed the executive order, of medical and nutritional aid for children. An emotional former USAID employee recounts how 500 pounds of food destined for starving children was already on the ground but could not be distributed because of the government veto, meaning it was allowed to pass its expiration date and then be destroyed. Musk himself provides the key to comprehending how people in power could be so heartless when he calls empathy “a bug in Western civilization.” His rants about the “woke-mind virus” are both disturbing and tiresome, and his flair for self-dramatizing outrage is illustrated by comments about his trans daughter, Vivian Jenna Wilson. “My son Xavier is dead,” Musk famously said, using his now-estranged offspring’s birth name. “Killed by the woke-mind virus.” Perhaps the loudest alarm set off by Gibney’s movie is the section devoted to Musk’s complete turnaround on AI. After initially coming out as a skeptic, he pivoted to full-steam-ahead with minimal regulation once he established his xAI offshoot — which quickly landed a contract with Pete Hegseth’s ignominiously renamed “Department of War.” Then there’s his chatbot Grok, which malfunctioned and self-generated an anti-Semitic, pro-Nazi rebrand dubbed “MechaHitler,” not to mention generating nude images of real women and girls. title: ‘Musk’ Review: World’s Richest Man, And His Digital Avatar, Thrashed In Damning Alex Gibney Doc – Venice Film Festival
full_text: Skip to main content By Matthew Carey Matthew Carey Documentary Editor, Awards @mattcarey More Stories By Matthew The Talk Of Telluride: Secret Screening Of Elizabeth Holmes Documentary ‘You Can See Everything’ ‘Musk’ Teaser-Trailer: World’s Richest Man Called “Chaotic, Capricious,” “Manifestly Cruel And Selfish” In Damning Alex Gibney Doc Director Pawo Choyning Dorji, Cellist Yo-Yo Ma Team On ‘A Song For The Snow Lion’ Set In Himalayas Of Bhutan – Telluride Film Festival View All September 8, 2026 5:05am 'Musk' Courtesy Bleecker Street What sort of billionaire criticizes another billionaire for giving tons of money to charity? The same kind of billionaire who would gleefully gut USAID, calling it a “criminal organization,” a move that has cost hundreds of thousands of lives, according to multiple estimates. What kind of entrepreneur falsely claims to have founded Tesla, when it was really two other men? The same kind of man who would claim to have held his dying infant in his arms, when it was actually his wife who did (a wife he later dumped). That’s the Elon Musk portrayed in the documentary Musk , which just held its world premiere at the Venice Film Festival . Related Stories News Alex Gibney Encountered "Tremendous Sense Of Fear Of Talking" As He Researched Bombshell Doc 'Musk'- Venice Documentary 'Musk' Teaser-Trailer: World's Richest Man Called "Chaotic, Capricious," "Manifestly Cruel And Selfish" In Damning Alex Gibney Doc The film depicts the world’s richest man as petty, narcissistic, megalomaniacal, cruel, detached from humans at a personal level (including various ex-partners and many of his children) while purporting to want to save humanity by colonizing Mars. A real prince. Musk , in my view, gives Elon the takedown he richly deserves. Watch on Deadline Elon Musk leaps on stage with then Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump in 2024. JIM WATSON/AFP via Getty Images At 225 minutes, some will deem it too long a haul, but I found the film engrossing from the start and a necessary length to confront Musk’s immense impact on contemporary life and politics, sprawling businesses, and complex personal life. The documentary’s most brazen and innovative technique is to turn Musk into a CGI avatar, enthroned in the purple glow of a digital background, eerily mouthing words that, as the film says, Elon has said in real life. He’s dressed in a tough guy leather jacket, dispensing self-justification and deep thoughts like, “I wanna be out there exploring the stars… I just want to know what’s going on.” He also speculates that we humans might be in a simulation created by some other being (to my mind a bizarre flight of fancy which subtly gives him license to ignore suffering on Earth. Hey, if we’re just characters in some grand intelligence’s video game, why be bothered by what happens to individuals even on a mass scale?). ‘Musk’ director Alex Gibney Courtesy of DOC NYC Gibney, who has applied investigative rigor to Enron, Scientology, Casino Jack Abramoff and other targets in previous films, digs particularly deep into Tesla and its safety claims associated with self-driving technology. The documentary asserts Musk has vastly overstated the capacities of Tesla vehicles, dazzling 60 Minutes ’ Lesley Stahl and other journalists with displays of his electric cars proceeding under their own guidance, while hiding a frightening reality. It explores cases of Tesla owners who let the car do the driving, only to die in accidents or kill others on the road (like a 2019 incident in Florida when a Tesla S model ran through a T-intersection, killing 22-year-old Naibel Benevides Leon and injuring her boyfriend). The film suggests Tesla lied about not being able to access data from its vehicle that struck Leon. Experts in the film also say Tesla has lied about the true range of its vehicle batteries and that it fraudulently promised to create a network of roadside ports where drivers could easily swap batteries, extending range (this dodge allegedly allowed Tesla to pocket millions in government subsidies predicated on the viability of the program). More darkly, Musk implies Elon wants the vast data a Tesla can accumulate on its owners to feed his AI ambitions. The documentary spends considerable time exploring Musk’s checkered romantic relationships, including with Justine Musk, his first wife who bore him six children (including the ill-fated Nevada, the boy who died at 10 weeks old from sudden infant death syndrome). He has rejected his trans daughter Vivian, one of his kids by Justine. The “pro-natalist” Musk has also sired three kids with the singer Grimes (aka Claire Elise Boucher), a baby mama relationship that has also soured. L-R tech journalist Zoë Schiffer, director Alex Gibney, and Ashley St. Clair attend the photocall of ‘Musk’ at the Venice Film Festival on September 8, 2026. Tiziana FABI / AFP via Getty Images One of the most absorbing parts of the film involves Ashley St. Clair, the conservative influencer, who bore a son by Musk in 2024. She chillingly describes encounters with Jared Birchall, a man often described as Musk’s fixer/enforcer, charged with muscling people like St. Clair under control. She refused to accept a financial settlement after her split with Musk that would have required her to sign a non-disclosure agreement; in lieu of an NDA, she freely speaks with the filmmaker about Musk in very unflattering terms. St. Clair was involved with Musk during the time of the 2024 presidential election when Musk, as we all saw, threw his arms around Donald Trump and leveraged his vast wealth to help get Trump reelected. In the film’s most sensational claim, St. Clair says Musk told her he would exploit “an anomaly in the matrix” to affect the outcome of the race, citing his access to space lasers – an apparent reference to his network of Starlink satellites. Gibney lets it hang that Musk might have nefariously determined the winner of the presidency. I found this less than completely convincing, though I would love to see definitive proof. Musk , to my mind, is most successful at painting a psychological portrait of the multi-billionaire. Musk’s father, Errol Musk, is interviewed in the film and relates a telling incident in which the family drove by the scene of a man who being resuscitated by the side of the road. Errol stopped the car and he recounts how Elon, then a boy, kept reading his comic book, completely ignoring the life-and-death drama in front of him. His childhood in South Africa is explored, one where the potential for violence in the country’s Apartheid era seems to have traumatized young Elon. He comes to Silicon Valley in his 20s and in short order has made millions from startups, including Zip2 (a kind of digital yellow pages), and X.com (not to be confused with his later acquisition, Twitter), a financial services and internet bank that merged with PayPal. In interviews back then, Musk comes off as awkward, a geek in pleated khakis with a receding hairline and uneven teeth. Before long, his wealth and his hair would expand, and the teeth would be straightened. This insecure Musk dwells within the adult who craves constant attention through his social media platform and reacts with fury to perceived slights (the film suggests Musk turned on Democrats in part because President Biden didn’t invite Tesla to an electric vehicle exhibition at the White House). Donald Trump and Elon Musk, speak in the Oval Office of the White House on May 30, 2025. Getty All this leads to Trump 2.0 when the reelected president handed vast power to Musk by appointing him chief of “DOGE,” the spurious Department of Government Efficiency. There, Musk’s disturbing lack of empathy would glory in slashing jobs and spending, including on the vital USAID. The full catastrophe of DOGE hasn’t been written, but Musk goes some way in exposing its arbitrary nature, grotesquely inflated claims of cost-cutting and utter failure as Trump negated any savings by handing a gigantic tax cut to the wealthy, ballooning the national debt. Most sinister of all, the documentary suggests Musk’s real goal in getting into the White House was to access data on all Americans, once again to feed his pernicious AI dreams. The Musk of this film is unscrupulous, power-hungry, and narcissistic, the child of a distant, difficult father. No wonder he and Trump bonded – until they didn’t, but then they did again, realizing they needed each other: Trump to get access to that colossal wealth and Musk to avoid government investigations into his enterprises and to maintain access to the federal piggybank and untold troves of data. Alex Gibney has made a lot of vital documentaries. This is his most important. title: BBC Strike Threat Rises As Matt Brittin Laments “Disappointing” Decision By Unions To Reject Improved Pay Offer
full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake Tom Jones Claims He Has Been Fired From ‘The Voice UK’ Because Of “Financial Difficulty” BBC Strike Threat Rises As Matt Brittin Laments “Disappointing” Decision By Unions To Reject Improved Pay Offer Harry & Meghan Briefing War Breaks Out Within Days Of UK Return; Couple “Surprised” By King Charles Edict View All September 8, 2026 4:47am BBC boss Matt Brittin BBC EXCLUSIVE : BBC boss Matt Brittin has revealed that unions have rejected an improved employee pay offer, increasing the likelihood of a mass staff walkout at the British broadcaster. In an internal town hall briefing, Brittin said the BBC had revised its pay increase offer from 1% to an average of 2.1%, but this was dismissed by unions, including the National Union of Journalists. “That was disappointing,” Brittin said. “I understand the cost of living and the pressures that people are under, but [I’m] just disappointed because people want clarity and we want to be able to give the pay rise.” Related Stories News BBC Rejects Complaints It Aired "Too Much" Coverage Of Harry & Meghan's UK Return News Richard Osman Appears To Confirm 'The Celebrity Traitors' Premiere Date Amid Talk That Season 2 Was "Intense" To Film The BBC director general said the pay talks had been a “pretty difficult process for everyone” and he acknowledged that industrial action was a possibility. Watch on Deadline Brittin said low earners would benefit most from the remuneration offer (some employees will get a 2.5% raise), while members of the BBC’s top leadership team will not receive a pay rise. He added that the BBC was making the offer in the context of cutting costs by £500 million ($675 million), while at the same time having no certainty over its future funding amid charter renewal talks with the government. Brittin said a 1% pay rise was equivalent to 180 jobs. “That’s where we’re in a tight situation on savings. How do we get the right balance between helping people progress with the cost of living, but also managing the size and shape of the BBC for the future.” BBC News presenter Adam Fleming, who was hosting the staff Q&A with Brittin, asked: “Do you think that people who want a bigger pay rise are putting their colleagues’ jobs at risk?” Brittin responded: “I understand completely why people want to be paid in a world of cost of living increases and so on. But yeah, that’s the choice that you have to make at a management level. To award more, you’re going to have to find the money from elsewhere. The cupboard is bare. There isn’t a cash reserve that we can draw on here. So that’s the kind of trade-off that we’re having to look at.” The former Google executive, who earns £565,000 running the BBC, said talks with unions would continue. He added that some union leaders were in favor of approving the 2.1% offer, but “different people have got different opinions.” Brittin said more details on BBC cuts would be announced in the coming weeks. The corporation’s £500M target expands on a previous savings goal worth £1.5 billion. The bigger picture behind the cuts is that 94% of the UK population use the BBC every month, but fewer than 80% pay the £180 annual licence fee. The BBC is attempting to bridge this gap. title: Elon Musk’s Ex Ashley St. Clair on Rejecting a $40 Million NDA and Participating in ‘Musk’ Doc: ‘I Hope the Risk in Trying to Fight Back Helps a Little Bit’
full_text: Sep 8, 2026 4:37am PT Elon Musk’s Ex Ashley St. Clair on Rejecting a $40 Million NDA and Participating in ‘Musk’ Doc: ‘I Hope the Risk in Trying to Fight Back Helps a Little Bit’ By Rebecca Rubin Plus Icon Rebecca Rubin Senior Film and Media Reporter rebeccaarubin Latest Elon Musk’s Ex Ashley St. Clair on Rejecting a $40 Million NDA and Participating in ‘Musk’ Doc: ‘I Hope the Risk in Trying to Fight Back Helps a Little Bit’ 2 hours ago Summer Box Office Breaks All-Time Record With $4.67 Billion 19 hours ago Ellen Burstyn Cries as She Gets Venice Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement: ‘It’s One Thing to Win an Oscar, Tony or Emmy — All of Which I’ve Won. But This Is a Lot’ 23 hours ago See All Michael Buckner Elon Musk ‘s ex Ashley St. Clair spoke about her decision to reject a $40 million non-disclosure agreement after the influencer gave birth last year to Musk’s 13th child. By turning down the alleged payday, St. Clair was able to sit for an interview in “Musk,” a new documentary from Alex Gibney that seeks to make sense of the controversial billionaire who has outsized influence on the world in which we live. “When you are offered something like that, it creates a debate about what your speech means and how valuable that is,” St. Claire said at a Venice Film Festival press conference for “Musk,” which premieres on Tuesday. “Why do they want to offer me this amount of money to not speak?” Related Stories Wim Wenders Clarifies His Stance on Filmmakers' Role in Politics After Berlin Controversy: 'We Are the Opposite of Politicians ... We Are the Antidote' St. Claire participated in the doc to “set the example for my kids that we should never take being materially comfortable that we’re speaking the truth,” she said. St. Clair gained prominence as a right-wing political commentator who advocated for conservative and anti-trans politics. She is now expressing her regret for platforming those beliefs, which she chalked up to her youth and confidants at the time. Popular on Variety “I got involved with Republican politics when I was 18 after I met Charlie Kirk, and there was an air of ignorance,” said St. Clair, who is now 28. “But that ignorance does not excuse any role in that. I hope the risk that I’m taking now in speaking out and trying to fight back at least helps a little bit.” Gibney, an Oscar-winning documentarian, has investigated corrupt corporations (“Enron: The Smartest Guys in the Room”), sexual abuse coverups in the Catholic Church (“Mea Maxima Culpa: Silence in the House of God”), Scientology (“Going Clear: Scientology and the Prison of Disbelief”) and alleged Russian interference in the 2016 U.S. presidential election (“Agents of Chaos”). Gibney began working on a film about the tech titan and world’s richest man, with an estimated net worth of $900 billion through ventures including SpaceX and Tesla, back in 2023. “The thing that struck me most, particularly early on, there was a tremendous sense of fear of talking — both among people who were his critics, colleagues and friends,” saidGibney said. “I talked to many, many, many people. Many declined to speak.” Gibney and St. Clair were joined at the press conference by another interview subject, tech journalist Zoë Schiffer. “Musk,” which premieres at the festival on Tuesday, is nearly four hours long — and Gibney joked he didn’t set out to make such a long movie. “We intended to make a shorter film before Musk became wrapped in the career of Donald Trump and the United States,” Gibney said, adding the first thing he did was reach out to Musk, who declined to be interviewed. “Musk” promises to reframe all we know about him, “revealing that the so-called ‘visionary genius’ is little more than the 21st-century reincarnation of a confidence man,” according to the synopsis. Musk himself has said that perceived reality may be nothing more than a simulation, and Gibney argues “even his most heralded accomplishments are rife with illusion and misdirection.” Musk’s recent ventures include buying Twitter (and renaming the social media platform X) and starting xAI and its chatbot Grok. Although Musk didn’t participate in Gibney’s doc, he long ago called the film a “hit piece.” Gibney called Musk a “very dangerous” man and expressed a deep worry about Musk’s unwillingness to show concern about other people. “I would say he has a very difficult time with empathy, especially cognitive empathy, which is putting himself in the shoes of others,” Gibney said. “He seems incapable of doing that.” Added St. Clair, “He makes a conscious choice to not put himself on other people’s shoes. title: ‘Musk’: Alex Gibney Shares His Take on Elon Musk’s “Global Right-Wing Agenda” and the “Almost Existential Fear” of Talking He Encountered: Venice
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All September 8, 2026 4:33am Zoë Schiffer, Alex Gibney and Ashley St. Clair (left to right) Courtesy of Kate Green/Getty Images Elon Musk took the spotlight at the Venice Film Festival on Tuesday. Well, not in person! But he and his influence took center stage as filmmaker Alex Gibney discussed his new doc, simply called Musk , during a press conference around lunchtime. The film about the owner of X and CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, world-premiering in the Italian fest’s Venice Open – Out of Competition program, comes from producers Jigsaw Productions (Gibney, Jessie Deeter, Erin Edeiken), Closer Media (Zhang Xin), Anonymous Content (Nick Shumaker, Jessica Grimshaw) and Double Agent (Dana O’Keefe). Related Stories Movies Laura Poitras and Rachel Lauren Mueller on Making ICE Doc 'They're Here' Like a "Horror Movie" Movies Why Andrew Garfield Says Billionaires Should Be "Scared Sh**less" by 'The Uprising' Despite its 225-minute running time, the Venice synopsis of the doc is brief and to the point: “An incisive look behind the legend of Elon Musk, the world’s most heralded ‘inventorentrepreneur’ who exerts an enormous influence on the world in which we all live.” Gibney shared how the doc team reached out to Musk for the film, without success, and how the focus of the project changed once the tech mogul “got wrapped into Donald Trump” and his story. The result is a mix of “the reality of what he has done and the unreality of his narrative,” the filmmaker said. “In the service of that, we created this formulation that came out of Musk’s own ideas about the notion that we’re living in a simulation or in some kind of existential video game, to convey in formal terms, through a kind of avatar, which speaks with Musk’s actual words, and video game imagery” both sides, the reality and the unreality. Of course, a member of the press asked if Gibney is concerned about a potential legal backlash by Musk. “We consulted our lawyers, and they gave us a sign-off to go forward,” when the doc team decided to use Musk’s words and visualize the mogul as an avatar, he replied. Asked if there has been any retaliation against the filmmakers, the director shared that he encountered a “tremendous sense of fear of talking, really almost existential fear,” among many of the people that the film team reached out to. So, how dangerous is Musk, especially for the future of democracy? “Extremely,” Gibney concluded. “Very dangerous.” A couple of questions focused on the tech mogul’s support for political parties on the right flank of the political spectrum in such countries as Germany, where the far-right AfD just won a regional election in Saxony-Anhalt this weekend. In fact, Musk congratulated the party on the victory via a “Well done!” on his X. Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s lead candidate in the region, thanked the billionaire in return, posting: “Thank you, @elonmusk , for your support and for your clear and highly important perspective on the political developments of our time — including here in Germany. If we take responsibility here, I would very much welcome the opportunity for strong and constructive cooperation. Germany would once again be a place worth investing in.” So, what does this all mean? “I hope I showed in the film that he’s involved in right-wing political parties all over the globe – in Germany, in the United Kingdom, in Brazil, in Turkey, and I think there are a number of reasons for that,” Gibney told the Venice press conference. “That seems to be his ideology at the moment. But in addition to that, many of these right-wing governments tend to be more pliable, and it’s easier to buy the results you want for administrations that are utterly corrupt and venal and have no sense of restraint or internal checks and balances.” Gibney’s takeaway: “So, I think he’s pursuing a global right-wing agenda, both for ideological and for very practical and monetary reasons.” Suggesting that these players are “more pliable,” the filmmaker emphasized the “crony capitalist aspect to his political aspirations” during the press conference. “With Trump suddenly, and with many other right-wing leaders around the world, he sees the possibility of being able to buy influence that’s unprecedented, because they’re much more amenable to the crony capitalist idea.” Gigney’s conclusion was that Musk is “always pragmatic” and “moves where the money is.” Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk walks to the stage to speak alongside Republican presidential nominee former President Donald Trump at a campaign event at the Butler Farm Show, Saturday, Oct. 5, 2024, in Butler, Pa. Alex Brandon/AP Images Gibney was joined during the press conference by political commentator and author Ashley St. Clair, who has a baby with Musk, and technology journalist and author Zoë Schiffer. The latter pointed out that at his companies, Musk tends to ensure “loyalty” at the highest levels,” while treating other people “pretty harshly.” At X, “he has tweaked the algorithm both to suppress mainstream journalism and to augment some of the more inflammatory comments and voices on that platform,” she said. St. Clair mentioned her past claim that “I was offered the opportunity not to speak for $40 million” in the form of a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) when she had her baby with Musk. “I got involved with Republican politics when I was 18, after I met Charlie Kirk, and there was an air of ignorance,” she explained. “But that ignorance does not excuse any role in that. I hope the risk that I’m taking now in speaking out and trying to fight back at least helps a little bit.” She also shared her take on his work with X and political parties around the globe. “His most complicated relationship is with the truth,” she said. “He is stoking flames that don’t exist in the real world, and he is creating something that is causing real-world effects. … I do believe that he is causing deliberate division that may be catastrophic if it’s not regulated or tamed, or if we don’t do our part in putting it down.” Gibney and St. Clair both mentioned what the former called Musk’s “very difficult and traumatic childhood” as a potential driver for him and his focus. “I think to some extent he’s now playing out that trauma on the rest of us.” All in all, he called Musk “a cautionary tale” that tries, among a “bewildering world of inputs” in the social media age, to stitch together a narrative to show the forest amid all the trees. In a director’s statement on the Venice website, Gibney shares: “In Musk , I chose to re-tell a familiar biographical tale but to forgo the master. Instead, I explored it from different angles that showed the master shot to be an illusion, and revealed a more disturbing truth. Musk reframes the story of the tech titan as the 21st century reincarnation of the confidence man. By subverting Musk’s favorite tropes of video gaming and simulations, the film conveys the dangers of becoming like the Game Master in Ready Player One . It’s a tale of power and its abuse.” THR

title: Alex Gibney Encountered “Tremendous Sense Of Fear”  While Researching ‘Musk’;  Praises “Brave People” Like Ashley St. Clair For Agreeing To Talk
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow , Nada Aboul Kheir September 8, 2026 4:27am Ashley St. Clair, Alex Gibney and Zoë Schiffer attend the 'Musk photocall at the 83rd Venice Film Festival Kate Green/Getty Images Oscar-winning director Alex Gibney told a Venice Film Festival press conference on Tuesday that he came up against a “tremendous sense of fear” as he canvassed for interviewees his new bombshell documentary Musk about controversial tech tycoon Elon Musk. “There was a tremendous sense of fear of talking, really almost existential fear, both among people who were his critics, people who were his business colleagues and people who are his friends,” he said. “I talked to you know many, many, many, many people who, except for some of the brave people here with me here, declined to speak.” Related Stories News 'Company': First Footage Revealed For Casey Affleck's Venice Drama Featuring His Two Sons Documentary 'Musk' Teaser-Trailer: World's Richest Man Called "Chaotic, Capricious," "Manifestly Cruel And Selfish" In Damning Alex Gibney Doc He suggested that the documentary had intersected previous works such as the Oscar-nominated Enron: The Smartest Guys in the Room , or his 2019 Elizabeth Holmes exposé The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley . Watch on Deadline “What I discovered was that the story of Musk was not, in a way, a new tech story. Though there’s much about it that is tech, but… his story is really the story of an old wine in a new bottle. His story turns out to be the story of the confidence man, the stock pumper, his wealth and power comes from inflated stock, and so I had told that story before with Enron and with Elizabeth Holmes, and so it was a story that was oddly familiar to me,” said Gibney. Gibney was joined at the press conference by Musk interviewees Ashley St. Clair, Elon Musk’s ex-partner and the mother of one of his children, and journalist and writer Zoë Schiffer, author of the 2024 book ‘Extremely Hardcore: Inside Elon Musk’s Twitter’. Asked why the had agreed to participate in the film, St. Clair brought up a previously reported $40M NDA offer she received from Musk after their relationship ended. “When you’re offered something like that, it really causes a debate in your head about what your speech means and how valuable that is, and why do they want to offer me this amount of money to not speak?,” she said. “And I believe Alex spoke to it a little bit about Elon’s unreality, and he does complicated relationships generally, but his most complicated relationship is with the truth. And so, I think most importantly, I want to set the example for my kids that you should never take being materially comfortable over speaking the truth.” View this post on Instagram Schiffer said her involvement chimed with her own work as a journalist who has covered Musk in depth, suggesting it was easier to find people who would talk further down the chain in “Musk Inc”. “His empire is that he has a lot of loyalty at the upper echelons of his company. He stacks the boards with friends and colleagues, but at the lower levels he doesn’t do a lot to engender a ton of loyalty toward him,” she said. “He treats people pretty harshly, and particularly when he’s coming into a new organization like USDS or Twitter. I think there’s a feeling that it’s a sort of takeover, and people who were there previously feel like something really wrong is happening, and those people were quite quite willing to talk. Overnight the production released a first trailer giving a taste of the film, with soundbites describing Musk as “chaotic”, “capricious” , “manifestly cruel”, “a nuke” and “a “fascist” Musk had yet to respond to the trailer by the time the press conference kicked off at 12.30pm CET (3am PT), having pre-emptively fired off a post on X on about Gibney and the documentary last week. title: Levan Koguashvili Brings ’90s Georgia to Venice With Comedic Drama ‘Guria’
full_text: Sep 8, 2026 4:25am PT Levan Koguashvili Brings ’90s Georgia to Venice With Comedic Drama ‘Guria’ By JD Linville Plus Icon JD Linville Latest Thomas Heise’s Final Documentary ‘Übergang,’ a Potential Locarno Highlight, Reflects on Time and Transience 1 month ago Low Light Films Boards Locarno Competition Thriller ‘O Jacaré,’ Basil Da Cunha Celebration of Lisbon’s Vibrant Reboleira District (EXCLUSIVE) 1 month ago Annecy Young Audience Award Winner ‘Into the Forest’ Finds Freedom Through Imagination 2 months ago See All 'Guria' Courtesy of Venice Film Festival Levan Koguashvili ‘s “Guria” will world premiere in Venice’s Spotlight section on Sept. 9. The black-and-white tragicomedy, set in the western Georgian Guria region, follows Zuriko, a 45-year-old widower and farmer as he struggles to find love, as well as a fair price on hazelnuts. “Guria” is a co-production between Georgia ‘s Kino Iberica, Switzerland’s Cineworx, Luxembourg’s Tarantula and Bulgaria’s ArtFest, with support reaching further afield, including Turkey’s Ministry of Culture and Tourism, Norway’s SoRFond Film Fund and Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea Fund. Related Stories Wim Wenders Clarifies His Stance on Filmmakers' Role in Politics After Berlin Controversy: 'We Are the Opposite of Politicians ... We Are the Antidote' It’s the director’s fourth feature, following “Street Days” (2010), winner of a Tiger Award at Rotterdam; “Blind Dates” (2013), which scooped the Special Jury Award at Abu Dhabi, and “Brighton 4th” (2021), which took prizes at Tribeca and Cottbus. “Guria” was written by Koguashvili with Boris Frumin, a former professor and longtime collaborator. Popular on Variety Variety spoke with Koguashvili in Venice about “Guria” ahead of the film’s premiere. This project is a seven-country co-production with global financing. Can you discuss how Guria came to interest so many parties in telling a Georgian story? Koguashvili : Basically, the idea of bringing in so many parties came from financing. We had to look for many co-producers. In our case, you get a little bit of money from different places. Of course, it’s harder to manage a production when so many people are involved, but on the other hand, it makes for a very international crew. You have a sound guy from Switzerland, an editor from Luxembourg… it’s fun. I was really grateful that people got interested in this crazy story about friendship and love in Guria and found support in different countries. And Saudi Arabia came in at the very last moment. We were still raising money for some pickup shoots, and we brought the film to the Red Sea industry park and showed 20 minutes. We won a couple of awards there, and that’s how the Saudi co-producers came on board. It was a really great help, at the very last moment. Can you talk about co-writing the film? What did that collaboration look like, and what did each of you bring to the story? Koguashvili : Boris was my professor at NYU’s graduate program, and we ended up becoming friends and working together after school. There’s a an age difference (he’s almost 80 now), but we started collaborating during my first film there, and it’s kept going ever since. The way it works: I bring the material, Georgian scenes, life situations, characters, protagonists, and we discuss what to do with it, how to connect the story. What matters most is having strong scenes. You need a handful of very strong, cinematic scenes, and the rest can be good around them. So I lean hard on that. Boris is great at organizing and constructing material. He’s very much a teacher in that sense, about the logic of story development, and that’s what I learned from him. I loved his classes, in terms of how he approaches structure. What about Georgia and Guria in the ’90s make it the time and place to anchor this story? What has changed about that world? Koguashvili : I like Georgian provinces very much because they still have an authentic feeling. Big cities look alike everywhere now, but the provinces have their own flavor, and Guria especially has a very strong character. So it was already somewhere in my mind. Then I happened to read a book, “Gurian Diaries.” It was melancholic, about the poverty and the humor of that time, but there wasn’t really a story in it, just a guy remembering his childhood. I liked the atmosphere, so I called the author and asked if he had a concrete story. He didn’t, but he suggested we go to Guria together and see what we’d find. I spent maybe two or three months there. Once I felt I had enough material, I took everything to Boris, and in about three days we had the shape of a story, a plot. Your work tends to straddle this line of hardship and comedy. What draws you to that place, finding light in the darkness? Koguashvili : Several things, maybe, but mostly, this is how I see life. I don’t see even tragic moments as complete tragedy; life is always full of dimensions. By introducing irony and humor, you don’t make a tragic story less tragic. It just gets a different feeling, it becomes more human, and it’s easier to digest. It also gives the story a kind of lightness and lyricism, which I love. I believe tragedy and drama have to be told with some comedy in them. You try to find levity or humor even in the darkest, most dramatic situation. It’s also a way of working against cliché: when you think of the ’90s in a post-Soviet country, you picture a very dark movie, right? But I think that’s become a cliché too, and working against it is its own challenge. Also, Georgian character isn’t simple. Georgian life in that period was extremely difficult, but there was also a kind of absurdity to it, even a charm. So many things, but usually the films I love have that quality. They’re all comedies about tragedies. It’s a very tragic story, but the telling of it is full of comedy. How did you come to use singing and song as such an important narrative tool in Guria? Can you talk about the songs the characters sing through the film? Koguashvili : Georgia has a very strong tradition of folk singing, and Georgian singing is polyphonic. Usually there are three voices, but depending on the region, some songs have five, six, sometimes seven parts. It’s very complex, almost like Stravinsky, in a way. If you listen closely, it’s an absolute improvisation, done by people with no formal musical education, just peasants improvising, but creating enormously original music. Singing is also very much part of Georgian culture more broadly, of the Georgian dinners we call supra, when people gather around the table. I grew up in a family where we had those dinners often, 20 or 30 people coming to the house, drinking wine, and singing. So for Guria, I met a very interesting composer, the head of a folk center who works with traditional folk musicians. I told him I wanted to do something in the Georgian tradition but approached differently, not polyphonic, but a single voice, because a single voice felt more intimate to me. He’s from Guria himself, so he understood what I meant.
